traveller to tlie destruction of tho trees on tho mountains. When tho war of liberation broke out, agriculture was neglected, and tbo wood from the hills being no longer required by human industry, a great jungle began to prevail over all The result was. that within twenty years,

not only had the lake ceased to subside, but began once more to rise and threaten the country with general þÿinundation. Other eases precisely similar might be cited ; but we take one in which there were means for measuring the alterations. At Marmato, a mining district amid dense forests in the province of Popayan, a decrease of the streams that drove the stamping-mills was observed, proportionate to the clearing of the woods. The mills served as gauges, and gave pretty accurate measures ot the diminution, which went on to such an extent that, at the end of two years, there was an anxious cry : What shall we do for water? The defect was the more unaccountable, as the fall of rain had not diminished. The clearing, though sufficient to cause a local disturbance, had not affected the general climate. By way of experiment, the cutting i and in the ditches, now runs down of the woods was stopped ; and gradually the rivers resumed their former flow. In the tropics, this result would naturally be produced more rapidly than in northerly latitudes: the quick-growing vegetation sheltered the soil, checked evaporation, and the surface-water, retarded in its flow, found its way slowly and steadily to the beds of the streams. The same thing has been noticed around Rio Janeiro : the terrible droughts which at times afflict the Cape de Verd Islands are attributed to loss of wood ; and in Madeira, a change of climate has been observed since the island was first discovered, from the same cause. There is less

humidity than formerly. The Socorridos, the largest river, was at oue time deep enough to float timber to the sea ; while now, except in occasional floods, it is a mere rivulet, scarcely discernible in its loose stony bed. The soil of Madeira is so light and porous, that it speedily suffers from deprivation of moisture The fact was early noticed, and a law was passed forbidding the cutting down of trees near a spring or source of a stream ; but as Portuguese laws are too often disobeyed, the evil has gone on increasing. The foliage is of a nature to favour a large deposit of dew; so large, iudeed, as to keep the ground underneath constantly moist. Thus, the trees become condensers between the atmosphere and the earth. The well-known trees on Ferro, one of the Canaries, present undoubted evideuce as to the condensing function. They are always j wrapped in a cloud, from which they so rapidly and effectually draw off the moisture, that a continuous stream flows down the stem into | reservoirs made to receive it. They are perennial fountains for the inhabitants, who prize them highly. Every one has heard of the destruction of trees in the Spice Islands by the Dutch, who, to increase the value of their monopoly, cut down nearly all the spicebearing woods, and thereby converted the islands into deserts : even now, those once luxuriant ocean-ringed oases have not recovered from the effects of such wicked waste. At Penang, the Chinese settlers make such reckless havoc in the clearings, that the English

governor has prohibited any further cutting down of trees on the hill-slopes. These slopes are too steep for permanent cultivation, and the Chinaman was content to get one crop from the virgin soil, and then clear another spot; but this shortsighted process is happily checked Besides the effect on the climate, the trees preserve the soil on the abrupt declivities from being washed away. To come to Europe : springs that once flowed in the highlands of Greece, have disappeared since the trees were cut down that formerly sheltered them. þÿ In þÿSwitzerland, says Dr. Balfour, þÿ has it been perfectly ascertained, that rivulets formerly full have shrunk or dried up coincidently with the denudation of the mountains, and that they have once more returned to their former size on the woods being þÿrestored. It appears to be certain that the planting of trees on the slopes of the French j Alps has prevented the occurrence of the þÿ torrential þÿfloods that once devastated the lower valleys. We may add, but without attaching any importance to it, that Pliny mentions the occurrence of contrary instances, where, by the cutting down of trees, the water that had nourished their roots bubbled up to the surface in springs. þÿCassander troops, s he remarks, were struok by those outbursts while felling timber for their intrenohments on the Balkans. Another consideration presents itself: besides the dearth of fuel and water, consequent on the de crease of forests, there are the danger and
destruction from torrents and floods that follow as a natural consequence. As Humboldt says: 1 The beds of the rivers, remaining dry duriog

s T . C If 0 I n avis- , a part of the year, are converted into torrents whenever great rains fall on the heights. The sward and moss disappearing with the brushwood from the sides of the mountain, the waters falling in rain are no longer impeded in their course; and instead of slowly augmenting the level of the rivers by progressive filtration, they furrow I during heavy showers the sides of the hills, bear down the loosened soil, and form those sudden inundations that devastate the þÿcountry. Clearly, civilisation and nature do not always go hand in hand in the promotion of social interests, as we may see in our own highly cultivated country. Forests we have none to speak of; but improved drainage is attended at times with consequences such as are mentioned above. The rain-water, instead of lingering on the fields off so rapidly that the rivers cannot discharge quickly enough, and the consequence is an inundation. In some places, there are ten floods now for one formerly. The farmers on the levels of the eastern counties of England can tell of how many times their hay has been drowned in the course of a single season. But to return to the forests. In St Helena, the quantity of wood has been considerably increased of late years by planting; and, as careful observation shews, the quantity of rain has increased þÿ almost doubled since the great Napoleon was a prisoner at Lougwood. And now the destructive floods, which used to follow every storm, have entirely ceased. Iu 1849, there had not been one for nine years;

nor have we heard of any since. In the neighbouring island of Ascension, as the report states, þÿ b a eautiful spring, situated at the foot of a woody mountain, was observed to diminish in flow as the trees were cut down, and to vanish altogether when the wood disappeared. After a few years, during which no water flowed, the mountain became wooded again ; the stream began to run, and, as the vegetation increased, resumed its former þÿvolume. We have abundaut evidence of a similar kind from India þÿ a country where the phenomena occur oil the grandest scale. The average yearly rain-fall along the shores of Hindostan is from sixty to eighty inches; but in the interior, at elevations 2000 to 4500 feet above the sea, it amounts to 200 inches. On the great plateau, however, and in places scant of trees, the fall is not more thau from ten to thirty-five inches, The change is not gradual, but sudden: of little wood, you may safely predicate little rain. Humboldt mentions the great plain he travelled over between the Andes and the Orinoco, as extremely arid and desert-like, though, according to the early settlers, it was once well watered and sprinkled with forests. Scarce as wood is in some parts of India, it is so abundant in others, that any recommendation in favour of economy is treated with a laugh. Protect the forests, indeed! Let us take a glance at what goes on iu the magnificent teak-forests of Tenasserim and Malabar. The Parsee merchants go with their woodcutters, and chop down

spars of from five to nine inches diameter, and seventy-five feet long, without regard to the future condition of the woods, and with so little regard to the demand, that one observer saw hundreds of these spars rotting on the beach. In the Canara forests, the jungle-people þÿ girdle the largest, as the Americans call it, and set fire to the rest? and then, without stirring the soil, sow millet or castor-oil among the blackened strumps; and after taking one or two crops, repeat the process in another spot. Thousands on thousands of acres have been destroyed in this way. þÿ Far as the eye can þÿreach, says Superintendent Onslow, þÿ not a tree is to he seen. It may be þÿsupposed, he continues, that clearing þÿ the forest would make the country more healthy ; and so it would, if the clearing were more permanent: but the forest is now destroyed only to be replaced by a thick jungle of rank vegetation, still more þÿunhealthy, as it impedes the circulation of the air. In some of the clearings, it was found that scores of sandal-trees had been destroyed, worth from five to fifteen rupees apiece, and gamboge-trees innumerable. The more intelligent among the natives of this Mulnaad ( rain-country) complain of want of rain: the fall is not of the same amount as formerly. þÿ To give you some idea of the waste of valuable and ornamental timber in this þÿcountry, says Captain Harrey, in one of his letters, þÿ will I just mention what I discovered at Hyderabad. I was in want of light-coloured wood for picture-
frames, aud applied to the rigimental contractor. What was my surprise to find that every third or

fourth log in his great store of firewood was most beautilul satin-wood of large size! Only imugine the victuals of a whole regiment, not to say of a large community, being cooked with satin-wood þÿ! Look also at what took place on the demand arisiug for gutta-percha as an article of commerce. Two hundredweights of this useful product were exported from Singapore in 1844 ; but sucli was the increase, that, in three and a half years from that time, not fewer than 270,000 trees were felled for the sake of their sap, without a single effort being made to replace them. According to Dr Cleghorn, the natives were thinking of abandoning a tract about fifty miles from Coimbatour, which had lost its rain through the loss of trees. Dr Gibson, who travelled through part of the Bombay presidency, after an absence of fifteen years, saw great changes for the worse, aud from the same cause. A similar change has bcou noticed iu the Neilgberry Hills. The proprietor of a coffoe-plantation near Bangalore, þÿ when clearing fresh ground which was watered by an excellent spring, was warned by the natives not to clear away the trees in the immediate neighbourhood of his spring: he disregarded their warning, cut down the trees, and lost his stream of þÿwater. Such instances are numerous, as also those ol clearing ravines for cultivation causing the disappearance of the brooks that once flowed refreshingly through them. From Afghanistan to the Burmese frontior, the phenomena have been observed as cause

and effect. Such an accumulation of facts forced itself on the attention of the authorities in India, and a system, on a small scale, has been commenced for restoring, at great labour and expense, what has so long been wasted. So far the results are satisfactory. The plantations formed along the line of the Jumna Canal very soon paid their expenses, and become every year more valuable. The natives have fallen in with the plan of establishing large mangrove gardens, and improve the trees with gaol grafts supplied by the government. Mr Tucker, one of the European residents, has placed a gold medal at the disposal of the Horticultural and Agricultural Society of India, to be given to the planter of the greatest number of trees iu the Agra presidency. In some places, regular plantations of teak are commenced as fast as the full-grown trees arc cut dowu. Those measures once taken, the consequences could hardly be other than beneficial in a country where wood is the universal fuel, and the consumers arc numbered by hundreds ot millions. The very thinnings repay more than tiie cost of management. It thus happens that the recommendations of the committee of the British Assosciation for þÿ careful þÿmaintenance, for the þÿ establishment of þÿnurseries, the checking of waste, and the planting ot woods on þÿ tracts unsuited for þÿculture, have bceu to some extent anticipated. But much remains to be done before the þÿtill balance between physical and social requirements will he maintained Tito alarming d. ficiency of rain

around Bombay during the last monsoon is attributed to the destruction of the forests. And in another point of view the preservation of trees becomes of importance þÿ namely, as regards shade. In hot climates, the þÿ boundless þÿcontiguity of the 1 :afy canopy is appreciated with a teeling to which we of the teinparate zone arc strangers. þÿ In the p ist ages of India, this thing was cared for. On instance will suffice. During the reign of Akbar, direction was given þÿ that on both sides of the canal down to Hissar, trees of every description, both for shade and blossom, be planted, so as to make it like the canal under the tree in paradise ; and that the sweet flavour of the rare fruits may reach the mouth of every one, and that from those luxuries voice may go forth to travellers, ealliug them to rest in the þÿ cities where their every want will lie supplied Before concluding, we must just mention that an attempt has been made to throw further light on the question by direct experiment. The particulars, supplied by M. Bdgrand, are published in the Annnaire of the Meteorological Society of France for ls53, and give the results of twenty þÿyears observation in the hilly parts of the Paris basin. The author shews that the nature of the soil, as to permeability, has to he takcD into account as well as the nature of the vegetation. Results obtained in our climates would not be strictly analogous with those of the tropics, where the leaves never fall, unless the experiments were made in some of the great
European fir-forests, which retain their resinous foliage all throughout the year.

tions, to recall her Minister or her Consuls at the dictation of a foreign Power. We have apologized for the faults we have committed. We have temperately and fairly pointed out the worthlessness of the proof of other faults, the commission of which we deny, and for which we can consequently offer no reparation. 'Phis we have done, but we can do no more. The Queen of England has offered to the United States such reparation as one great Power may fairly and candidly make to another; but this nation will never suffer the posture of its Sovereign to he changed from one of cordial and candid friendship into an attitude of enforced humility and unworthy deprecation. This nation would exact a heavy account from any Government which it should think has, by rashness or want of consideration for the feelings of its neighbours, compromised the peace of the world ; but it will be equally resolute to maintain, if driven to extremity, its honour and independence. Observations precisely similar apply to our difference with the United States respecting Central America. In order to disarm their jealousy we have voluntarily assured them that we have no intention whatever of seeking for aggrandizement or extension of territory in that quarter. We differ in tin1 interpretation of a treaty, and have repeatedly offered to submit that treaty to the arbitration of any friendly Power. More than this we cannot do, unless, in order to avoid collision, we surrender our own interpretation of the treaty, and submit to one

which we know never to have been contemplated by our Plenipotentiary. This we cannot do, and it will therefore be for the United States to consider what purpose it will serve to push us any further on this subject. We will not suffer ourselves to suppose that there is any truth in reports which have reached us that the internal affairs of the Union have arrived at a point which renders it necessary to seek in foreign war a diversion from domestic discord. Such wild and dangerous counsels are unworthy the position and alien from the spirit of the great Transatlantic community, whose wisdom and fortune it has been to wring from peace conquests more successful and more durable than have ever been attained by the most successful war. History affords abundant instances where the unprincipled ambition of powerful States has urged them on to provoke an unequal conflict with smaller and weaker communities; but that a State should rush into war with another at least its equal in all those resources which are necessary for military success, while that country, so far from offering any provocation, is exhausting every expedient instance ened collision, is indeed an to avert the threat- ol conduct which we do not care to characterize further than by the observation that it is totally unparalleled in history. Let us for once, we trust without arrogance, venture to propose our own example to the United States as one not wholly unworthy of imitation. When the dispute with

I We feel authorized without alleging specified arguments to state our conviction that whilst aDy division of the legislative power in colonial matters between several representative Assemblies in the Mother country, the members of which are not conversant with them, must in general be yet higher degree inappropriate and when injurious, this is the case in a such a division is effected iu branches or the legislation which are apt to come in frequent inward contact with each other, and that this truth in particular applies to the division proposed by the Diet, we will explain under No. : 2, By the intended repartition of the colonial revenues and expenses into two Budgets the Custom- and Ship Dues, Fort Charges and Post Revenues are entered iu the common Revenue Budget, and the other colonial revenue-items in the þÿ special þÿBudget. We reserve to ourselves to show iu the progress of our remarks, that this division is not entirely in harmony with the rule of the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult. 4, when applied to the colonial affairs divided according to the conception of the Diet into common and special ones. But what we in this stage of our observations have to urge first of all, is that a division of the Colonial Budget whatsoever, and the sanctioning of such division on the part of several legislative powers will without leading to any imaginable beneficial result, exercise a very detrimental influence upon the future development of the Colonies, which essentially depends upon an improved arrange-
ment of the direct and the indirect taxation in the Islands, not exclusively in the interest of the State Treasury, but just as much in that of the

resp Land Treasuries. The general revision of the system of taxation, which also in harmony with the communications from the Government to the Colonial Council can soon be expected to be carried out, will, particularly as far as St. Croix is concerned, lead to a remodelling of the direct taxes on estates, so that the resp. would have to be transformed into an import-duty on estate supplies, hitherto imported duty-free. This alteration, which will have to be enforced by one and the same law, would however, as far as the abolition of the direct tax is concerned, would according to the proposition belong to the province of the Diet, and to that of the Imperial State Council with regard to the new custom-revenue, and the reciprocal relations between both these Budgets in regard to their final averages must then show very different results, as the same amount which now as Ground Tax will form one of the special would when collected in the form of an importduty belong to the general revenues. It has in the Diet been justly urged that the export-duty imposed on the produce of the Island by the Ordinance of the 1st October 1802 must in substance be considered as a production-tax on the estates of the Island and as such it is designated in 13 of the Draft of a Law on the St. Thomas Commerce and Shipping laid before the Council in the session of 1854. When a division of the direct and the indirect taxes is to be consistently carried out, we must agree to class the export-duty amongst

We look forward with anxiety to the arrival of the second June Packet, due at St. Thomas to-morrow, in the expectation of placing before our readers later intelligence from Europe in connection with the vexed questions that are at present occupying the serious attention of the Governments of Great Britain and the United States, and which threaten a rupture between those Powers. The same mail may also bring us word of some final arrangement being concluded in relation to the Sound Dues Question, as it must be remembered that the 14th of June was the day appointed by the United States for a definite settlement of that question. EUROPEAN. From the London Times, May 28. AUSTRIA. Vienna, May 24. A few days since yon learnt from me | ritory and authority that the Austrian Government was likely to give to the world an account of the origin and object of the treaty April of 15, and the subjoined article, which is contained in the Wiener Zeitung of this morning, affords satisfactory proof of the correctness of my statement: þÿ þÿ An international document þÿ the treaty concluded on the 15th of April, 1856, between Austria, France, and Great Britain þÿ which first became public when presented by the British Cabinet to of Par- liament, has induced the organs the press, of all lands, to indulge in conjectures of the most various kinds. Suppositions have been made, and consequences deduced which have frequently been in keeping neither with the sense nor with the object of this important treaty. In order to place both facts and principles in their proper light, we will give a briel account, as well of the circumstances which led to the conclusion of the Treaty of April 15th as of its object. þÿ The mutual guarantee of the integrity of the Turkish Empire was not introduced into the Austro-Anglo-French preliminary points, the acceptance of which by the Russian Court led to the peace now so happily concluded. During the Vienna Conferences, the Russian Plenipotentiaries so a positively declined to take any share in guarantee that the introduction of any such clause into the fundamental conditions must have rendered it extremely difficult to bring mat-

ters to a satisfactory termination. At the Paris Conferences it was the very same case. The principle (of a mutual guarantee) was, however, most distinctly laid down in the treaty of December 2; it was to outlive the war, and to take its place among the most firmly based international treaties. The war was neither waged for the sake of conquest nor from interested motives, but solely for the re-establishment of satisfactory international relations. Without such a guarantee as that above-mentioned, the peace and quiet of Europe might again be disturbed. France, England and Austria interfered in the struggle between Russia and the Porte; the first with the sword, the last by means of military demonstrations ami treaties. The principles which united them (the three Powers) were unchanged, and, therefore, the international alliance was consolidated in a most conservative sense after the war which had led to it was at an end. þÿ It was neither for Austria nor for the Western Powers to demand of the Imperial Russian Cabinet during the cal negotiations for peace that it should, in contradiction to the former positive declarations of its representatives, share in an active guarantee. Neither could the contracting parties do otherwise than hesitate to invite the Prussian Government to take part in the matter in question, as Prussia had, during the whole course of the Eastern difference, announced and maintained its resolution not to enter into any kind of obligation which could at a future time interfere
with its perfect freedom of action. It is true that the treaty of April 15records the continuance of an alliance, an intimate union, between France, Austria,

C i 0 I 1 V !: and England, but it is based on the principles justice, of which the Sovereigns openly profess, and which in no way either menace or injure any other Government; the treaty is based on principles which support and protect ter- balance of power in Europe and the the of the Governments of all countries. 'File treaty of April 15th, by its contents and sense, is a guarantee that the parties to it will nowhere and never swerve from the principles of international law and justice. þÿ Such an alliance requires no secret conditions, no reserved clauses, for the purity of its tendency will justify it in the sight both of the present and of future generations. Indeed, we are in a position to affirm that there are no secret articles whatever to the treaty of the 15th of April of this year. þÿ We cherish the firm persuasion that although the treaty in question secures the prolonged union of Austria, England, and France on the principles of law and justice, it in no way interferes withlhe most intimate federal relations with Prussia and the other German Stales, nor prevents the complete re-estabhshmentof sincere, friendly, and neighbourly relations with Russia. þÿ Vienna, May 23, 1856 þÿ The foregoing official article contains little more than has already been said in my correspondence, but I have given it in extenso, as there are some slight peculiarities about it, to which your attention will now be directed: þÿ 1. The alliance with France and England has given Austria the courage to use plain

language, so that there are none of those vague phrases which may be interpreted according to the taste of the reader. 2. It is insinuated that the treaty of April 15 would not have been concluded if Russia had thought fit to place her sincerity beyond all doubt. 3. Whenever the names of the Allied Powers are mentioned together, either the last or the second place is allotted to England. This to foreign readers may appear the result of chance alone, hut such is not

the position of every word, is duly considered by official Austrian writers. 4. Such a favourable opportunity of þÿ having a þÿhit at Prussia has not been neglected. 5. By the concluding passage of the article it is to be presumed that the relations between Russia and Austria are at present neither friendly nor neighbourly, and the language employed by the Russians in this city is well calculated to remove all doubt on the subject. We must therefore declare our conviction, that to divide the superior administration in the Colonies would be an even more, detrimental measure than to split the Colonial Government at home, and it is a pervading sentiment in the colonists that nothing could possibly be invented more conducive to weaken public security and destroy all confidence in the future than any division or retrenchment of the Governor's official authority. On the strength of all these arguments urged by us against the alterations in the principles hitherto observed in regard to the legislative power over the Colonies and to the colonial administration, which either are contained in or flow from the Bill of the Diet, we must most positively dissuade from its being carried out,

and we feel convinced that the Diet, after having acquired a due knowledge of the practical circumstances which so strongly militate against its enforcement, will desist from furthering the Bill. The communication by which it is accompanied involves a strong inducement for the Colonial Council, in case the Diet should arrive at such a conclusion, to enter a proposition of such an altered arrangement of the matters in question which would be likely to obtain the approbation of Ilis Majesty the King and of the Legislative Bodies of the Mother Country. Previous to advancing our views in this respect, we only feel the more called upon to express our opinion on the original Draft presented by His Majesty's Government to the Diet the 30th December ult., as it does not appear clear from the Debates of the Diet, that it should be unconditionally or ultimately given up on the part of Government. The said Draft contains that " the interior affairs of the Colonies are not to belong to the separate, affairs of the Kingdom of Denmark," and therefore purports by an alteration of the Enactment in the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult. to arrange the matter thus that all those colonial affairs which hitherto, agreeable to 2 þÿ 1 of the Colonial Law, are submitted to the legislative power of the King and the Diet, should henceforth belong to the legislative power of the King and the Imperial State Council. The explanations which accompany the, Draft e,xpre,ss, besides pointing out the impracticabi-
lity of a division of the Colonial Budget hitherto collected under one, amongst others, that, whilst the Colonics originally have been ac-

IWr. 54. quired by sacrifices on the part of and for the entire Monarchy, and the revenue-surplus arriving from tliein has accrued to the general State Treasury, which ou the other hand has had to hear in the individual years considerable loss caused by them, the inhabitants of the different parts of the realm have thus long since been put on a par in regard to the advantages which private, subjects derive from the possession of the Danish West India Islands. Though we readily acknowledge, that the objections started by us against the Bill proposed by the Diet are not applicable to that presented by the Government, and that the latter, at least to a certain degree, tends to maintain that highly desirable singleness of of legislation and administration, we cannot acceed to the Bill of the Government and will take the liberty of stating our reasons at large : 1, It is a self-evident fact, that the Colonies are just as much as all the other parts of the Monarchy comprised under the constitution of the entire Realm, and we from our colonial point of view do not entertain the slightest doubt, but that the interests of the Islands will at the hands of the legislative power of the Monarchy experience that conscientious care which they have to claim as forming one of the manifold objects belonging to its province. The Draft in question however purports to place the Colonies in a position to the entire Realm, totally different from that of any other province of the Monarchy, and when we have

reserved to ourselves to prove, that the Fundamental Enactment of the 2nd October ult., is not adapted to introduce such a position, we cannot retrain from expressing here, that the Draft, to judge from the concommitant explanations, seems to proceed from a rather incorrect notion respecting the position of the individual provinces of t lie Monarchy to the Colonies. At the period when they tirst began to he subjected to the dominion of the Kings of Denmark, in 1671 and in 1734, and even in 1754 when the then existing Danish West India Company, up to that time the owner of St Croix, was redeemed by the State Treasury, only a very scanty portion of Holstein belonged to our Kings, and even that formed a part of the German Empire. The conjunction of the Colonies with the rest of Holstein since 1773, and with Lauenburg since 1816 can certainly, considering the great surplus-revenues notoriously derived from the Islands, not have entailed any losses upon those provinces, though the increase of the National Debt caused by the compensation granted for the losses occasioned by Emancipation, must now be deducted from that nett surplus. The Colonies have, generally speaking, solely through the Kingdom of Denmark been attached to the other provinces of the Monarchy : it is through Denmark alone that they have been brought into colonial relations with the other parts of the realm, and should ever, which we trust will never come to pass, the link of connection between those provinces

be severed, these Islands will unquestionably have to follow Denmark, in perfect unison with what in the Documents executed by the Members of the Royal Family in regard to the Stic cession to the Throne lias been expressly stipulated, that the Colonies belong exclusively to Denmark proper. It does not appear to stand in harmony with these political arrangements, that at the same time when the Constitution of the entire Realm in all other respects, as at present, only concerns certain distinct affairs which all the provinces have in common, general any " Territory" with the totality of and whilst no individual part of them or in its affairs is subjected to the new legislative authority instituted by the Constitutional Law of the 2nd October ult., this should quite exceptionally take place in regard to the Colonies, as it they stood in no connection whatever with any of those provinces and as if they much less would be placed on an equal footing with them, but must in each and all be incor porated in the entire Realm.

2, Whereas according to the Ordinance of the 21 si March 1755 the Danish is in substance anu reality to be the Law of the Land in the, Islands, and the Danish High Court their Supreme Tribunal, it would from this reason alone be inconsistent to refer the Departments of Justice and Administration of the Islands to the Constitution of the entire Realm instead of to the Diet. 3, It has evidently not been the intention that the legislative authority instituted by the constitutional Law of the 2nd Octr. ult., should obtain actual force in any part of the Monarchy on the totality of its affairs, nor can the special Lnactments of it be said to be adapted to to such a plan. We will in this respect call the attention of the House to 48, in virtue of which the power of imposing new taxes vested in the Imperial State Council only regards such taxes which the entire Monarchy has in common, as also to 52, concerning a "Normal Budget" and separate additional Budgets for each biennial financial period. But above all we have here to urge that the rule laid down in 31, that the Imperial State Council shall ordinarily only be convoked every second year, might engender a very detri- I the Custom Department has become a general mental procrastination in colonial legislation, j and we apprehend that its development on account of the innate discrepancy between the same and the rest of the affairs which constitute the sphere of action of the Imperial State Council will not be duly attended to.

4, The Imperial State Council is not invested with the same privilege granted to the Diet by 48and 50ofthe Fundamental law of taking the Initiative to propose new laws and of appointing Commissions of Investigation, and the right at present inherent in the inhabitants of fairs. the Islands, of having any Bills, which the Government, though applied to in unison with 5 of the Colonial Law refuses to enter upon, brought before the Diet, would thus be lost. 5, Lastly we must express, that the popular influence which the Diet will always exercise upon the Government cannot in the same measure be attributed to (lie Imperial State Council, and if it be admitted ' that the Colonics undoubtedly have tl connection with the Law, it must also < taken for granted that Kingdom to thank I i r their present Colonial any future development of their in the legislation concerning themselves will proceed safest and lu st under a continuation Croix and St. of the position to the Diet which they have hitherto held. When we have thus dissuaded from the adoption of the Government Draft and have now to investigate, in what other manner a suitable arrangement of the position in which the Colonies have been placed to the legislative power of the Mother Country by the Constitutional Law and the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult., might be effected, the starting point must be to render perfectly clear the real nature of this position and this depends upon the interpretation of the words : "the in-

terior affairs of the Colonies." We have in the earlier stages of our statements only proved that the meaning cannot be : those colonial affairs which correspond with the separate affairs of the Kingdom of Denmark, but in order to arrive at a distinct definition of the notion itself we must partly refer to the verbal sense, partly to what, in harmony with the enactments in question, constitutes the contrary of such verbal sense. The words, " the interior affairs of the Colonies" simply and clearly imply the affairs comprised within the boundaries of the Colonies, of course also including their harbors and other maritime territory. According to the literal comprehension the legislation on these matters sequently would therefore not he confined to the Departments of Justice and Police, of Church and Public Instruction and the other matters recited in the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult., as far as they may be applicable to the Colonies but would in like manner have to be exercised on the Military Department in the Islands in general and not exclusively the, Militia Corps, on the Departments of Navigation and the Customs, as far as all Enactments to be observed in the Colonies themselves are, concerned, on all taxes and imposts levied there and on the Post Depatment in the. Islands. On the other hand their literal comprehension cannot imply such Custom- and Navi gation laws, which may contain Enactments

s T , C R 0 I X A V r s that concern the Colonies and perhaps most materially affect their interests, but which are to be observed in the Mother Country, and just as little such affairs which in general concern the Monarchy and the Kingdom and regard the Colonies merely as a part or as an annex of the same, f. i. the Department of the Navy, matters concerning the riglitD and privileges of the natives of Denmark, and the solution from the ties and duties of a Danish subject, or Treaties with Foreign powers regarding the Colonies etc. When we turn to examine the question, what the contrary of " the interior affairs of the Colonies" is, we meet nowhere a definition of "exterior" or "non-interior" colonial affairs. As the reverse can only be meant such colonial affairs which in unison with the Constitutional Law and the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult., are to be general affairs for the Monarchy. Even admitting that it on the whole is the province of positive Enactments to define the compass of such general affairs, still the notion is not purely arbitrary in itself, for general affairs must always remain those, which regard the principal portions of the Monarchy, the Kingdom and the Dutcliies in toto. long to the general affairs of the Monarchy. Referring especially to the financial Department, it harmonizes with what we have just now stated, and must result from the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult., that all the revenues as well as all the expenses hitherto entered in the Colonial Budgets, with the sole exception of the sum assigned to keep a Manof-W'ar in the West India Seas, must belong to " the interior affairs of the Colonies" and conto " the separate affairs of the Kingdom." It might be objected that the expenses <d' " the, Central Administration of the Colonies" in strictness do not appertain to the former affairs, but they must at all events belong to " the separate expenses of the Kingdom" in regard to the Colonies and be defrayed by them, and it is therefore completely in rule, that they are entered in the Colonial Budget. All the affairs constituting the province of the " Central Administration" will appear to belong to "the interior affairs of the Colonies." Captain Jardan, of the brig Hobart front Jacniel, arrived at this port, reports that on the night of May 21, in consequence of torrents of rain having fallen almost without intermission for three days preceding, the stream called Orange overflowed and submerged a part of the city, and undermined and carried away from twenty to twenty-five houses with persons in them, and several were drowned, while others escaped by boats. DRAFT of a Law containing certain modifications of the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October 1855, with special reference to the Danish West India Islands. 1. In accordance with the Royal Proclamation of the 2nd October ult , which refers þÿ the interior affairs of the þÿColonies to the separate affairs of the Kingdom, the exercise of the legislative power over the Danish West India Islands continues to be directed by the contents of the Colonial Law of the 26th March 1852, and a Financial law respecting the revenues and expenses of the Islands will in particular have to be sanctioned by the legislative power of the Kingdom The Financial Laws thus sanctioned as also the Financial Accounts for the Danish West Tndia Islands will be laid before the Imperial State Council. 2 The Surplus of the Finances of the Danish West India Islands accrues to the Finances of the Monarchy, which will in return have to cover any eventual Under-balance by extra-grants passed in due constitutional form.

Mr. þÿBaez administration, s unlike that of his Predecessors, was marked by acts, which demonstrated that he had a profound sense of the important duties imposed upon him by his election to the Presidential Chair. Of pleasing manners, agreeable deportment, and patriotic principles, his after conduct showed him to be worthy of the position to which he was elevated by the unanimous concurrence of his countrymen. Composed as the people were of heterogeneous materials, opposite interests were to be reconciled, private animosities softened if not allayed, and ridiculous distinctions þÿ which have ever been the curse of the colonial possessions þÿ abolished. This task w'as not an easy one ; but under his able auspices, the steady desire which he had to serve his country, made him rise supe rior to the difficulties of his position. His Predecessor Santana (I speak not of JtMENES, þÿSantana unworthy s successor), was a good and valiant patriot, and a sincere lover of his country, and had made considerable sacrifices to conquer its independence. But he was otherwise incompetent, illiterate, and devoid of that prescient foresight which, in discerning existing abuses, can at once suggest the required remedy. Guided by counsellors, not always disinterested, Mr. þÿSantana administration s manifested principles which were of a nature entirely opposite in themselves. At one time, exceeding the authority granted to him by the Constitution, in committing cruelties which were highly

condemnatory ; at another, relaxing his vigour in the timely prosecution of those measures absolutely- required by the necessities of the people. In fact, he was the. dupe of men wiser than himself, who flattered his follies whilst they abused his confidence. The administration of Mr. Baez, on the contrary, was of a nature to give the highest hope to his countrymen ; and it is gratifying to state,

Economy in a Family. There is nothing which goes so far towards placing young peoble beyond the reach of poverty, as economy in the management of their domestic affairs. It matters not whether a man furnish little or much for his family, if there is a continual leakage in his kitchen or in the parlour, it runs away, he knows not how, and that demon, waste cries þÿ more þÿ! like the horseþÿleech s daughter, until he that provides has no more to give It is the þÿhusband s duty to bring into the house, and it is the duty of the wife to see that none goes wrongfully out of it þÿ not the least article, however unimportant in itself, for it establishes a þÿprecedent nor under any pretence, for it opens the door for ruin to stalk in, and he seldom leaves an opportunity unimproved. A and look after his affairs, man gets a wife to to assist him in his journey through life þÿ to educate and prepare his children for proper stations in life, and not to dissipate his property. The þÿhusband sinterest should be the þÿwife s care, and her greatest ambition carry her no farther than his welfare and happiness, together with that of her children. This should be her sole aim, and the theatre ol her exploits in the bosom of her family, where she may do as much towards making a fortune as he can in the counting-room or the workshop. It is not the money earned that makes a man wealthy þÿ it is what he saves from his earnings. A good and prudent husband makes a deposit of the fruits of his labor with his best friend,

and if that friend be not true to him, what has he to hope V If he dare not place confidence in the companion of lus bosom, where is he to place it ? A wife acts not, for herself only, but she is the agent of many she loves, and she is bound to act for their good, and not her own gratification. Her þÿhusband s good is the end to which she should aim þÿ her reward. Self gratification his approbation in dress, or is indulgence in appetite, or more company than his purse can well entertain, arc equally pernicious. the The first fastens to extravagance ; second adds vanity a docþÿtor bill s to a long þÿbutcher account s ; and the latter brings intemperance, the worst of all evils, in its train.

From the London Weekly Dispatch. It is a fearful thing to doom a man, even judicially to put a Palmer to death ; what is it to execute a nation ? Far more, what is it to destroy a nation without right, contrary to law, reason, justice, written covenant ? Yet this is much what Europe, England as well as the other nations, is doing. Lord Lyndhurst, in one of those speeches which indicate the vigour and heart of youth revived by the repose of old age, brought the annihilation of the Polish State before the i louse of Lords on Friday. It was no stale repitition, no worn-out grievance in his hands, though he merely recapitulated the facts of the gigantic wrong. The Duchy of Warsaw created into a kingdom by the Congress of Vienna the two Emperors, Alexander and Nicholas, swearing preserve to its independence in all particulars as a separate sovereignty þÿ A letter from Parma, in the Risorgimento of the story of the annihilation of all these covenanted rights and of peijury in every particular, down to the miserable threat at the second Alexander in his address of Warsaw, and the mockery of an amnesty which he has proffered to the exiles þÿ are the subjects of Lord Lyndhurst's clear narrative, and the ground of his insisting that Lord Clarendon must, in conjunction with the French Plenipotentiaries, have done something to reverse all this ineffable wrong at the Conferences of Paris. Lord Clarendon's reply is a confession of impotence, and that is the epitaph of Poland. The House of Lords rings with cheers at the

old ex-Chancellor's appeal ; but it hears with complacency from him and from the Foreign Minister, that his denunciation can do no harm, because it pledges no one but himself. Lord Clarendon relics only on the tender mercies of the new Czar, as kindliness of his nature. " But, my Lords," Lord Lyndhurst hopes somewhat from the concludes Lord Clarendon, " I must say I believe that if the Emperor does intend doing anything for Poland, it must be spontaneous, and I believe that that country would derive little benefit from either Parliamentary discussion or the expression of individual opinion." The act is consummated. Europe will stand by and see one of its nations buried alive, engulphed as were the families of Korali, Datlian and Abiram. It is an awful fact. One man decrees the non-existence of a great people, and it is done. The millions are at his mere mercy. We do not say that we " believe" that this tyranny will be struck down and punished ; we know it. Not directly, perhaps, for the ways of Providence "are not our ways," but essentially and surely. Europe may be an assemblage of unmixed cowards but the retribution will come nevertheless. There is, however, something that men may for the future, do if they dare not redeem the sins of the past. We have just received (he " Address of the Students of the University of Turin to the Gentlemen of the English Press." After mere youths," they say, and can do no tendering most generous thanks, " "We are more than give this slight token of our re-

gard and gratitude. But the day is, perhaps, at hand, when the Italian youth, matured by age, may yet stand by Old England, and fight out the cause of political and religious freedom all the world over, and shew themselves worthy of the esteem of the free men of England of all parties." We accept the alliance. England and France have virtually pledged themselves to the regeneration of Italy by their acts at the Paris conference. The bargain shall not be paltered with. The honour of this country at least shall not be shivered into shapeless atoms by any trembling hand ready to let it fall. If the words spoken on our behalf meant nothing, those who

þÿ Scraps and Refuse Economised, The Chemistry of Art, like a prudent housewife, economises every scrap. The horse-shoe nails dropped in the street during the daily traffic, are carefully collected by her, and reappear in the form of swords and guns. The clippings of the travelling tinker are mixed with (lie parings of horses hoofs from the smithy, or the cast off woollen garments of (lie poorest inhabitants of the sister isle, and soon afterwards in the forms of dyes of brightest hue, grace the dress of courtly dames. The main ingredient of writing ink was, possibly, once part of the broken hoop of an old beer barrel. The hones of dead animals yield the chief constituents of Inciter matches. The dregs of port wine, carefully rejected by the port wine drinker in decanting his favorite beverage, are taken by him in the morning in the form of Seidlitz powders, remove of the bauch. The to offal the effects of his de- streets and the washings of coal gas reappear carefully preserved in the lady's smelling bottle, or are used to flavor Bi.ancmangks for her friends. This economy of the chemistry of art is only an imitation of what we observe in the chemistry of nature. Animals live and die þÿ their dead bodies, passing into putridity, escape into the atmosphere, whence plants again mould them into forms of organic life, and these plants actually consisting of a past generation,, form our present food.

From the St. Thomas Times, July 23. We inserted in our last an article taken from the St. Croix Avis. We have since been isked by the friends of equal rights why it was it had not been accompanied by a few remarks of our own. We have also been taken to task if our silence arose from the fear of " a power which punishes without a trial" or, to escape the " withering stroke of the Censor's mighty pen In truth, we must say, that it was not in tear of a power, which punishes without a trial, for such we do not know, but we certainly did wish to escape the latter ! However, as our silence appears to have produced surprise, we now assume the question. Early in 1852 the Colonies received a Report from the Committee appointed in Copenhagen to give an opinion on the Colonial Law ; that document was placed before the Diet by Count Sponneck, then the Secretary for the Colonies, who, in presenting the able instrument to the two houses, embraced the opportunity whilst talking of other matters to say, that it was his wish, it was also the wish of the Diet, and the Danish peop'e generally, that all matters of interest relating to the Colonies, should be freely discussed by the Colonial Press Actuated no doubt by such liberal, generous, and encouraging language, the Colonial Council, in its session thereafter, recommended by a vote of eighteen against iun, that the Press Law as promulgated with the Constitution in 1849, should be extended to the Colonies. How it came to pass that a minority of two was triumphant when the Council's

deliberations were brought before His Majesty for sanction, will long continue an enigma in the minds of those who have been taught to i wore the privileges of a fourth estate. The Censor here, until lately, with such proofs and opinions bofore him, had come to compn hend the Law of Censorship, if not posilivrh/ removed from the Statute Hook, should nevertheless, be seen in the light of a Law which time and the liberality of the age had made obsolete, and could only be acted upon where there was a predisposition to exercise it. Ilence it is, that in St Croix the Avis is enabled to say, the "influence of the Censor is mild," from the obvious reason that the weight of his pen is not known. For ourselves, so certain are we that the Censorship of the Press in the Colonies is only a question <f :i <, that we have never deemed it a case which required those herculean and sacrificing labours which were bestowed upon it by those patriotic spii its, who obtained its emancipation in the Parent State. We have seen that the enlightenment now possessed by the Colonists must make them entitled to the earnest solicitude of the Kingdom, and a wise policy will bestow upon them every form of government which their intelligence qualify them to receive. We fully know that their are a few in our midst who contemplate with alarm, the Liberty of the Press. But those very few do not see that their uneasiness results from their never having lived where a Free Tress exists, and front their public

positions, come to think that its pellets would be solely directed against them. These, however, are all nightmare visions, and when dealing with a general question like the Press have but little weight in the balance. Those who would understand the definition of " free press," would do well to peruse the following, written by an eminent English Barrister, in a late libel suit : þÿ "We now proceed, as we intimated at the beginning of this article, to lay down the doctrine which enters into every question of this kind, viz., þÿ that, if taking all the parts of a

S T C R 0 I X A V I composition together, it shall not be found to exceed the bounds of a free and fair discussion, so far as a regard to good order, the peace of society, and the security of the Government requires, but so free as the nature of our happy constitution, and the inalienable right of Englisluneu to discuss public affairs ; if, in short, the discussion be upon the whole sufficiently decent in its language, and peaceable in its import, although marked with great freedom of opinion, and couched in terms as animated as a free man can use on a subject that interests him deeply ; although even a great share of heat should be found in the expression, and such invective as, passing the bounds of candour and charity, can only be excused by the violence of honest feelings ; þÿ nay, although detached passages may be pitched upon, in their nature and separate capacity, amounting to liiiels, yet these also shall be overlooked, and the defendant acquitted, on the ground that he has only used the grand right of political discussion with uncommon vehemence. " This great doctrine forms, obviously, the foundation of whatever is more than a mere name in the Liberty of the Press þÿ the first and proudest pre-eminence of the first country in the world. An enlightened English Jury were once addressed as foil » w s, bv an illustrious being whose mighty genius was ever devoted to the cause of liberty, and they believed him and acted on his persuasion. lie said, that for using one or two intemperate expressions, one

'must not be subjected to infamy. If this severe duty were binding on your consciences,' said he, "th Liberty of the Press would be but an empty sound, and no man could venture to write f on any subject, however pure Ins pur- 1 i. pose, without an Attorney at one elbow, and (Jounsel at the other.' And, again, ' It is the nature of every thing that is great and useful, both in the animate and inanimate world, to be wild and irregular, and we must lie contented to take them with the alloys which belong to th m, or five without thein. Genius breaks from the fetters of criticism, but its wanderings are sanctioned by its majesty and wisdom; subject it to the critic, and you tame it into dull ess. Tempests occasionally shake our dwellings and dissipate our commerce, but they scourge before them the lazy elements which w ithout them would stagnate into pestilence. In ke manner, Liberty 1 herself, the last and best gift- of God to his creatures, must be taken just as she is. You may pare her down into bashful regularity, and shape her into a perfect model f severe scrupulous law, but she would then be Liberty longer; no and you must be content to die a d r the lash of this inexorable bannc.s of Freedom.' Just. , which you have " exchanged for the

" I conjure you to guard the Liberty oy the 1 ress, that great sentinel of the feratc , that grand detector of public imposture guard it ; b cause when it sinks, there sinks with it into one common grave the liberty of the Subject and the security of the Crown. þÿ Ccrrax."

How many Miles a Printer's Hand Travels. þÿ Although a printer only be sitting all clay, yet in his own way he is a great traveller (or, at least, his hand is,) as we shall prove. A good printer will set. 8,000 ems a day, or about 24,000 letters. The distance travelled over by his hand will average about one foot per letter, going to the boxes in which they are contained, and, of course, returning, making two feet every letter he sets. This would he a distance each day of 48,000 feet, or a little more than nine miles þÿ and in the course of the year, leaving out Sundays, the member travels about 3,000 miles. þÿ London Journal.

would be abandoned, and the countries on the coasts of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Persia, the eastern coast of Africa, India, the kingdom of Siam, Cochin-China, Japan, China, the Philippine Islands, Australia, and New Zealand the would he brought nearer to us on an average by 3000 miles. According to Mr. Anderson's calculations, the distance from the English

Channel to Calcutta, via the Cape of Good Hope, by the route taken by the best sailing vessels, may be put down at 13,000 miles; by the Mediterranean, the lied Sea, and the Indian Ocean, the distance is about 8000 miles; þÿ the Suez Canal would, therefore, shorten the passage to Calcutta by 5000 miles, and to Bombay 5300 miles, as compared with the Cape route. The railway now constructing over the Isthmus, though excellently adapted for the transit of passengers, the mail, and small parcels, will never be suited for the carriage of heavy goods, on account of the expense of loading and unloading at both termini. By the very great saving of time and distance between Europe and tlie East, our productive classes would come into more immediate contact with three hundred millions of Chinese and one hundred and fifty millions of people inhabiting the peninsula of Hindustan; and we should be able to send troops from Malta to Bombay in three weeks, to Madras in four, and to Calcutta in five weeks. In spite of the cost and delay attending the voyage round Capo Horn and tin- Cape of Good Hope, the yearly traffic now amounts to 6,000,000 tons; and it is not unreasonable to calculate on double that amount, could the course of navigation be directed through the Gulf of Arabia. Every country in Europe would benefit by the execution of this magnificent scheme. It would bring Holland nearer to Java and Sumatra, and Spain to tin- Philippine Islands ; while it would infuse new life into the ports of the Mediterranean, and per-

haps revive the ancient mercantile glory of the old trading cities of Italy. Prince Metternieh has long been aware that a ship canal through the Isthmus of Suez would powerfully promote the material interests of Venice and Trieste ; and indeed the whole of Germany and Hungary would reap considerable advantage from it, especially in conjunction with the canal projected by Mr. Wilson, the Dutch merchant, from the Danube to Kustendjeh on the Black Sea. We have now to consider the political results I of this colossal enterprise. How would it affect Egypt? Both France and England have I in turn held military possession of that country, and, on several occasions, it has caused uneasi- . ness to the diplomatists of Europe. The ruler j of Egypt would, of course, be master of tlie Suez and Pelusium Canal, as the ruler of Constantinople is master of the Dardanelles. As France and England united against Russia to prevent the Czar seizing the latter position, so \ would a combination arise aj.air.st any single Power that attempted to command the new | maritime highway between the lied Sea and j the Mediterranean. This prudent jealousy among the different nations of Europe would guarantee Egypt to the family of Mehemet

ambition, afford a solid security for the mainof peace in that part of tlie worl 1 It has been urged in some quarters that the project under consideration might endanger Britisli India, by facilitating the passage of a hostile armament to its shores. earth and good will to man. National debts favour in the world, nations will not slaughter

INTERVENTION IN ITALY. " It is not tvell to halloo till you are out of the wood" says the old proverb. The French and some of the English have been hallooing very lustily at the close of the war for the Inand generally dependence of the Turkey ; and the Austrians, friends and supporters of absolute government in every part of Europe, have joined in the chorus. But, nevertheless, Europe is still in the very thick and middle of a dark and tangled wood, unguided through the labyrinth by a single principle. There are dangers on a hundred sides, which those who are not blind can see ; and which will vet task the sagacity of statesmen, and the military power of Empires and Monarchies, to confront and subdue. The most palpable and obvious of these dangers lies in Italy. In that country the Nemesis which is to punish the Governments of Europe for playing fast and loose with the eternal principles of Justice begins to bestir herself. The potentates who have deluded themselves with the vain idea that a temporary truce is as good as a permanent peace, who have looked to the things of to-dav and taken no heed of those of to-morrow, will have to gird up their loins for new conflicts, and to prepare themselves to meet face to face the real question of the epoch. That question simnly means whether the various populations of Europe shall lie allowed to work out in their own way the great problem of constitutional liberty and national independence þÿ or whether a league of Sovereigns for the maintenance of

arbitrary power shall cover Europe with large standing armies hostile to popular freedom and incompatible with social progress, and whether they shall systematically repress all enlightened opinion and keep in a state of semi-barbarism some of the noblest regions in the world. Italy has raised the question. When Sardinia was admitted into the alliance of Great Britain and France, when her gallant array gathered its well-earned laurels on the bloody field of the Tchernaya, the Italians were fortified in the hope that the day of their deliverance was at hand, and that the grip of the foreigner þÿ as odious to them as the grip of Russia would have been to Turkey þÿ would be taken from their necks. That hope has not only bee i disappointed, but the cessation of the war, by freeing the armies of their oppressors from more stirring and more perilous work elsewhere, has led to more stringent tyranny and to more abominable misrule in everv part of the peninsula, except in Sardinia. Even that country, more favoured than the rest, has felt the intolerabl weight f Austrian neighbourship, and has been kept in a state of siege by the contiguity of Austrian armies, sent into and maintained in Italy with the avowed purpose of isolating Sardinia, and of repressing the natural desire for constitutional liberty and enlightened government of the noble-minded and unfortunate people of Rome, Lombardy, Tuscany, and the Two Sicilies. II"nce there is irritation on every side ; and Sardinia threat-

ened with bankruptcy and revolution by the pressure put upon her resources by the menacing movements of Austria, is prevented from working out her own system, and pursuing her own career of internal improvement. She is coerced and injured by the mere presence of the Austrian armies on her frontiers ; while every bad king and potentate in Italy is encouraged in his tyranny and oppression by the portentous apparition. If we may judge from the tenor of the most recent news from Italy, from the semi-official feelers which are put forth in French as well as in English journals that are known to be the organs of their respective Governments, or from the cautious statements that have been made by Lords Clarendon and I'almerston in the Houses of Lords and Commons, an intervention by England and France in the affairs of Naples seems to have been decided upon. There are people in England, and elsewhere, who ask what right England has to interfere in this matter ? and why the subjects of the King of Naples should not be allowed to settle the question with their Sovereign as they best can ! We agree with these persons that nonintervention in such cases is the safest rule and the wisest policy ; and that England has no more natural right to interfere with the King of Naples than it would have to interfere with the Emperor of the French or the Emperor of Russia, if either of these potentates were at war with his subjects. Non-intervention is

S T <. CHOI A V I s « what the Italian and all other European nations should demand ; but, unluckily, for them intervention is a fait accompli. Austria and France have severally intervened in the affairs of Italy þÿ the former to support its dominion over Lombardy and Venice, and to suppress those principles which, if allowed to spread in any part of Italy, would ultimately prove fatal to Austrian rule ; and the latter, with more questionable policy, to maintain upon his unsafe and mischievous throne a Sovereign who, but for that support, would cease to be a Sovereign and to maladminister the temporal affairs of the Roman people. The affairs of Italy would receive in due time their just and natural solution from the hands of the Italians themselves, if the Austrians and the French consented to withdraw their troops from Italian soil. Austria is not likely to retire from Italy, unless she be compelled to do so by force of arms ; but France is willing to recall her troops, for France has no p ditical objects to serve in Italy, and would be quite content to see the Pope reduced to a priest, and settled either at Avignon or at Jerusalem. It is of no use for Englishmen or Frenchmen to talk of non-intervention, unless they are prepared to remonstrate þÿ and, if need be, to struggle þÿ against þÿ lished an intervention that perpetuates mis- the intervention that is already estabrule, and that, by goading the Italians to revolt and revolution, keeps Europe in a state of ferment and insecurity.

It is clear that there must either be intervention or non-intervention in Italy. If non-intervention is to be the rule, then France aud Austria must cease to uphold the Pope and the King of Naples against the wishes of the Romans and the Sicilians ; and leave those populations to manage their own affairs. This would be the b st solution of the difficulty ; but, as it would lead to a successful revolution in those States, and consequently in Milan and Venice, it is not at all probable that Austria will consent to it. There are but two other courses to follow þÿ the first is to do nothing, but to allow the King of Naples and the petty despots who imitate his example, supported as they are by Austrian councils, to outrage every justice þÿ feeling of humanity, and every principle of G)vernment when the until Italian and human nature can endure no longer. Engineers know that boilers will burst under certain circumstances, and statesmen know quite as well that popular feeling will, under certain conditions, as certainly ex.Jode in blood and ruin. As the Governments of England and France are not prepared to countenance and encourage a course of conduct that would produce such a catastrophe, any more than they were prepared to allow Russia to overawe and coerce Turkey, the only course remaining to them, as the Powers most largely interested in the welfare of all Europe, and as the exponents and representatives of its civilization, is that they should intervene to secure for the unhappy Italians

the right to live, to prosper, and to enjoy the security of law and order. A King like the King of Naples is a nuisance, not only to his own country, but to the whole of Europe. If England and France intervene to make him just and reasonable, they will take the first step toward the regeneration of Italy. The Romans and Tuscans will then move for the same object; and perhaps Austria will learn that if she cannot maintain herself in Italy by the justice and wisdom of her rule, her bayonets will fail her in the ripeness of the time appointed; and that Europe will not consent to be always kept in a state of smouldering and contagious revolution because her statesmen have not the commonest sagacity or the most ordinary prudence.

THE CIVIL WAR IN KANSAS. The news from Kansas, which arrived on Sunday last, by the Royal Mail steam-ship Niagara, shows that the rebellion in that district is gradually extending itself. Despatches from a reliable source, which reached New York on the 13th ult., state that two Free-state towns (Ossawatomie and Palmyra) have been sacked by a pro-slaverv moh ; the most gross and unwarrantable excesses have been committed. Great numbers of Missourians were crossing into the territory, and committing depredations in every direction, without any effort on the part of Governor Shannon to stay

them þÿ one party having come under his observation without any comment. Colonel Sumner had succeed d in preventing the expected hattie at last advices, but could not disperse the belligerents. The investigating committee continued their labours, the testimony taken by them being of the most important character, and proving conclusively the ill gality of a great majority of the votes given at the election of the Kansas territorial Legislature. A telegraphic despatch, published in the Boston Advertiser ot tlie 17th ult., gives a melancholy account of the state of affairs in Kansas, and reports that there is fighting in all the inhabitable parts of the territory. It also reports that a very large body of men in Missouri are preparing for a descent upon Kansas, determined to drive out the Free-state men at all hazards. They expect little or no resistance, but it Colonel Sumner interfere they will drive him from the territory. I he most important proceedings in Congress relate to the civil war. In the Senate Mr. C rittenden moved to take up his resolutions requesting the President to appoint General Scott to the command of the United States' troops in Kansas. A discussion ensued, a number of senators maintaining that the presence of General Scott in Kansas would have a tranquilising and beneficial effect on the whole country. Others argued that such a request would be an improper interference by the Senate with the executive functions, and that the difficulties in Kansas would soon cease

if the people there would obev the laws, and the pefqde of the North would cease agitation. The subject was finally passed over. On a subsequent day Mr. Clayton offered another plan for the pacification of the Kansas. He proposes to abolish the existing Territorial Legislature and elect a new one, the voters to be bona fide inhabits ts of the territory three months, an.l of their respective districts one month, previously to the day of election. The laws of the territory relative to the discussion of the slavery question and the maintenance of the Fugitive Slave Law are also to be abolished. The people are authorised to form a State population shall have re rched the number af 93,120. This is the third proposition presented in the Senate for the settlement of the Kansas troubles. Mr. Trumbull wants to annex the territory to Nebruk i : Mr. i Irittenden believes < leneral Scott can restore tranquillity aino.g the squatter sovereigns ; while Mr. Clay Ion is in favour of taking a fresh start altogether.
