Another of your contemporaries puts forward some reflexions on the question, in connexion with the account that the United States have prolonged their treaty with Denmark of 26th April, lo26, for another year, dating from the 14th of June, when the first extension expired. Although the treaty here alluded to is included in the well known Marten's Rkcueil de Trai tes, 1 regret to say, that not a few of the organs of the English press are labouriug under total ignosance of its contents þÿ an ignorance most deplorable, not so muoh on account of the importance of the present subject, as because of the doubts which it gives rise to regarding the correctness of their information in general. As the treaty of 1826 is based upon the principle of reciprocity, and its provisions stipulate that American ships in Danish ports, with regard to the Sound dues and other matters, as well as Danish ships in American ports shall be placed on an equality with the most favoured nations, it is simply a contradiction to speak at one and the same time of an extension of the treaty, and of reprisals made on the part of America, by levying additional charges on those Danish vessels which enter the ports of the Transatlantic republic. Of two things one: either the term of the treaty is extented, and each nation is bound to treat the ships of the other in its ports ou an equal footing with the most favoured nations þÿ or the treaty is not prolonged, and the privileges enjoyed

in consequence of it have expired, and Danish ships must pay þÿ American ports while, on the other side, Ame- the highest dues imposed in rican ships are obliged to pay higher Sound dues, though they are at liberty to do so under protest, and reservation þÿ Tep.tium nos datur. Could states or nations be destroyed by strong and most improper abusive expressions, your coutein porary would, no doubt, long ago have annihilated ray fatherland- - so immoderate are the terms which he applies to a state that declares itself willing, on condition of a small indemnification, to waive rights based upon imuieiuoiial prescription, as aDo to the Euglisii government, because it has not (in reliance on a power which Deuuiaik could certainly not resist joiued the United States and the Chambers of Commerce i.i Germany in denying this right, and rel using ih,s indemnity. It is pretended that Denuiaik's right to "these piratical dues" have special treaties only, "which is based upon either run out their prescribed time, or may be abrogated by a simple notice." To this assertion I giv. a most unqualified denial. Every special treaty in existence might expire without Denmark's right to the Sound duos being in the least impaired therebv, for the treaties merely provide for the enjoyment of certain privileges and reductions of imposts as regards the powers concerned, and the consequences of their abrogation or expiration would therefore merely be to entitle Denmark to levy upon all flags the highest

duties which are now only levied on the flags of such countries as have not concluded treaties with her, as for iustance the States of C utral America, and, I believe, some of too Italian States. To me it seems passing strange that the Chambers of Commerce of Germany and the United States should be cited as examples for imitation. As for the German Chambers, they would do well first to agitate for the abrogation of the like " piratical dues" within their German boundaries, and more particularly the Stade duties þÿ and the exclusive concentration of their indignation on the Danish Sound dues is one proof the more of the spirit of enmity towards Denmark which has of lato years prevailed with the agitation against ' the Baltic black throughout Germany, and which has more to do mail" than people in England are aware of. Whether Great Britain would do well to follow the example of the United States in their assault upon the Danish Sound dues þÿ whether this nation would in the long run find itself benefited by any support given to the doctrines of the law of nations, such as they have been propounded by Mr. Maroy þÿ I leave to the judgment of those who have attentively followed the position taken up by the trans-atlantio republic during the recent and still fermenting misunderstanding with England. But the attempt of your contemporary to prove by means of statistical tables the crippling influcnoe exercised by the Sound dues

s T & k o r x A. y ii upon the trade of England with the Baltic has filled me with unutterable astonishment. From the fact that in 1S49 6,885 English vessels went to the Baltic, but that this number decreased in 1850 to 5.448 þÿ iu 151 to 4,811 þÿ and in 152, to 3,902 þÿ he draws the conclusion that it is the Sound dues that are the cause of the falling off. Supposing even that it never entered the writer's mind that since 1849, for reasons near at hand, a great part of England's trade with the Baltic might possibly have been carried on in foreign bottoms it might at least have struck him that the Souud dues did not commence in 1849, and that his conclusion is not only upset by the fact that the number of English ships trading to the Baltic had been gradually increasing up to that year, but also by the fact that the number of ships of all nations trading to those waters continued to increase after that year, and up to the period when the blockade of the Russian ports caused a change in the previous state of things. And now Sir, I come to certain statements concerning the Danish land and transit dues, contained in a letter from your correspondent in Lubeck, which appeared in your impressiou of Saturday last. I ain ready to acknowledge the friendly disposition towards Denmark evinced by your correspondent's expressions of satisfaction at the prospects of a peaceful issue of the difference with America, aud of an amicable redemption of the Sound dnes, though I much regret that in referring to the fairness of Denmark's

claim to 35 000 000 rix-dollars indemnity he should state the ordinary net revenue derived from the Sound dues as amounting to 1,000,000 rix-dollars, when in reality it is more than double, or upwards of 2,200,000 rix-dollars. I agree with your correspondent on several points relating to the land transit dnes levied by Denmark on goods passing through Danish territory from the North Sea to the Baltic þÿ but there are some errors in his statement which i must beg leave to correct. First, your correspondent is mistaken when speaking of these transit dues as couneeted with the general custom regulations for the whole monarchy, introduced a tew years ago (in 1.-53 J þÿ for these dues date, on the contrary, as correctly stated, from 1839, aud are consequently 15 years older than the regulations. Fuithur- 11 > < , it seems to me that the expressions "uuju.-t" rind "illegal," as app.ied to this measure, are u . lu'y v< ;e and hardly warranted. It may be doilbttui whether the special privileges of the Hinseatie towns did not preclude Deuuiaik from tht right of imposing these charges, aud the qu-'stion w.s in consequence souie years ago brought before the Germanic Diet, but was again withdrawn before the Diet could pronounce its verdict, a treaty with reference to it having be 'ti concluded on the 8th of July 1 40, between Denm irk and the Hauseatic cities, 11 .uiburg, and Luhcck þÿ and a measure based upon a treaty can hardly be called unjust, and at ail events cannot be termed illegal. I cannot stop further

to clucidite the nature and history of these charges but. I would refer those of your readers who desire further information on the subject to the " Oerrounia" of the 28th of May, ot tins year, a Heidelberg publication devoted to matters connected with the economical interests of nations, and in which it is treated with general correctness, though by no means in a manner favourable to Denmark. I must limit myself to declaring, that I know from a throughly authentic source, that the Danish government is only waiting for the final settlement of the Sound dues question, in order to proceed to a spontaneous revision of the Holstein land transit dues It follows as a matter of course that as soon as the abolition of the Sound dues has taken place, that amount of the transit dues which may be considered as an equivalent to the former will at once be repealed, and a sound financial policy, suoh as is acknowledged by the present liberal government in Denmark, will at the same time suggest further mitigations in this tax if for no other reason, in order to make it more lucrative than it is at present. Herewith I conclude the observations I have felt bound to make in common justice to my country, and which I trust will not be found without interest for English readers. 1 am persuaded that the attempts which are at present being made to abrogate charges which have for many years given rise to bitter complaints will ultimately succeed, and that it is desirable that they should succeed. Denmark has been so
moderate in her claims that none of the powers represented in the Copenhagen conferences have

found reasrn to object to the sums demanded þÿ and it must be allowed that leitmark could not demand less, if she were to be even tolerably indemnified for the expenses she has incurred, and will continue to incur, in connexion with tht navigation of those waters. For I must bee you to bear steadily in mind that not only has Denmark a prescriptive right to those charges which are now characterised as piratical extortion, but that she is every day acquiring new rights to the duty by her constant endeavours to render navigation easier and less dangerous. The tedious and dangerous voyage through the Cattegat to the Baltic is facilitated by means of excellent lighthouses and light-ships, and Denmark is on the point of carrying out a complete system of lighthouses, which will entail considerable ex penses on its annual budget, but which will render the illumination of one of the most dan gerous trade routes on the ocean as perfect as that of the populous streets of a city. By these measures, as well as by other endeavours for the benefit of navigation ( us, for instance, by the establishment of numerous stations provided with every means for the rescue of shipwrecked mariners, by publication of the excellent Dauish charts, dc ) the Danish government lias afforded the maritime nations a not quite insignificant equivalent for the charges which she now offers to commute for a fair indemnification. Three of the powers more intimately concerned þÿ viz., Russia, Sweden, and Norway þÿ have already

given their unqualified consent to her proposals. Other powers þÿ and among these more especially Prussia þÿ evince an increasing willingness to subscribe the terms prrposed. The United States, which at first assumed so threatening an attitude, have since then drawn back a little, and most, likely they have already officially recognised the principle on which the proposed indemnification is based. Those powers that are tarrying and hoi ling back have their eves fixed upon England, and it is she who in this instance as in so many others, will by her final resolution determine the rest of Europe The solution of the question depends in consequence upon England, and I confess that my < untrymen await the settlement in anxious suspinie. I will not on this occasion dwell upon the fact, that as a constitutional country Denmark is, as much as Sweden-Norway, obli -cd to sr. k in the West a support against the gr at Russian colossus, nor will I refer to the debt which England owes to Denmark since 10", when she crippled for a long period the power of resistance of the latter state. It is not my wish to appeal to the feelings or to the commiseration of other nations I appeal to justice and to the real interests of al! parties concerned þÿ and 1 will only add that by consenting to Denmark's proposal, of an indemnity of little more than 1, 000, 000, England will sa-e about the half of the anuual charges levied upon her ships, and the latter will, moreover, by the abrogation of the Sound dues, save

the triple and quadruple of this amount by avoiding detention at El.-inore, and the chance of losing a favourable wind and current The inquiries of the parliamentary committee have fully established these points, and there is reason to expect that its report will be favourable to a proposal which Denmark has made in consequence of remonstrances addressed to her during many years by the English government I am, d-c., 1) ANUS London, July 8

The Sound Dues Question. I he Loxmix Times, ol the 1st August, in a leading article of some length, reviewing the exaction of the Sound Dues hy Denmark, concludes with the following cogent and well-timed

remarks, almost every eye just now being turned towards England for an example in this matter : þÿ þÿ AVe assume that, while other nations eon tinue to pay, England will never avail herself of her superior strength to refuse this tax to a nation to whom she is bound by so many friendly feelings, by the memory of so much harsh treatment, undeserved by Denmark, and inflicted by England, under the spur of what, she believed to be a stern necessity, on a nation to whom the loss of this revenue would he so serious a blow, and whose independent existence is of the utmost consequence to the policy of England. þÿ Somehow or other, then, Denmark must he compensated for the loss of these dues ; but we would suggest that this compensation should close the matter at once and for ever, and not, like the plan of paying at the ports of clearance or discharge, leave the amount to grow with the increase of trade till it might well happen that foreign nations might have the honour of defraying the whole expenses of government all,l defence in the little kingdom of Denmark, which is endowed with no corresponding power ot self-augmentation. Having on F riday evening the 22nd inst., received a communication from the Road Inspector of the Southern District of Kings Quarter, intimating that Fair Plain Bridge is in a dangerous state, being the first intimation thereof, which I have received, I on the following morning directed by letter, the Quarter Officer to examine it, and order such dangers to be immediately repaired, but as that may be the work of time, and as besides the common traffic, many persons going to the race at the end of the week may have intended travelling this road, I give this public notice that they may take a different route to avoid crossing this bridge. St. Croix, 25th August 1856. AND. LANG, Chief Inspector of Roads.

From the Illustrated London News. PROGRESS OF THE SPANISH INSURRECTION. So tar as can be gathered from the most recent intelligence, the insurrection, instead of being nearly put down, as the Madrid journals have been pretending, is evidently spreading and assuming formidable proportions. The Madrid Gazette of the 25th July admits that " there are still several towns in the province of Granada in a state of insurrection;" hut it professes to feel no uneasiness at the fact, which it attributes solely to the circumstance of the troops being without " a leader, General Blanco having been most unexpectedly" taken prisoner by the insurgents at Jaen Private letters however, put the affair in a very different light. It appears that at Granada the National Guard, having obtained permission from the Captain-General to assemble, immediately assumed a hostile attitude. The troops sent against t hem "showed so much indecision" þÿ that is the expression used by a party favourable to O'Donnell þÿ that the Captain- General felt it necessary to " consent to an armistice of six days." In other words, he was constrained to allow the insurrection to organise itself. The National Guards put themselves in communication with various neighbouring localities, where risings look place, and General Blanco, who had been sent by Government to supersede the Captain- General on account of the " weakness" shown by the latter, was taken prisoner by the brothers Merino while attempting to reach his post. At Malaga the

troops joined the National Guards, and, headed by the civil governor, made their pronuneiamento against the amp d'etat- It is, however, reported that all the officers above the rank of chef de battaillon withdrew from their men. The latest news represents Almeria and Jaen as still maintaining a hostile attitude. Letters from Barcelona, of the 26th ult., received at Marseilles, state that General Zapatero held the town with a force of about 12,000 men, and that the streets had " nearly" resumed their oidinary appearance. The " greater part" of the factory operatives had returned to their work. Many, however, had "followed the insurgents," who have left town, and joined by the peasantry, scour the country, having for their headquarters the mountains in the neighbourhood of Barcelona. This is exactly what was feared. At the date of the 26th it was stated in Barcelona that Saragossa, having received from various quarters detachments which had " pronounced" against the of regular troops Government, formed a stronghold of resistance. It was added that the peasants of Lower Aragon were still marching in large numbers to join the insurrection at Saragossa, just as those of Catalonia rallied around Barcelona. These accounts go to corroborate the statement as to the formidable numbers of General Falcon's forces made by the Maniteur a few days ago þÿ a statement which it has never retracted, although it has published less authentic intelligence not easily reconcilable with it.

It is quite clear by this time that the stories of General Falcon having fled, of General Dulce having opened fire on Saragossa several days ago, and of his being in a condition to cut off the supply of provisions to the insursent garrison, were all inventions of O'Donnell's party.

THE NEW SPANISH DICTATOR. The personal courage of O'Donnell is j unquestionable, but it is not so much to ! that ordinary quality that he owes his j brilliant career as to the favour and protec- j tion of Espartero, who, in 1838, appointed j him Chief of his Staff. In 1840 O'Donnell embraced the cause of Maria Christina | against the people and the army, and j abandoning his command, he emigrated j with her to France. In 1841 he demanded j permission to return to Spain as a friend j to the established Government, and made j the most solemn declarations of harbouring no design against the public tranquillity. Espartero, then Regent, would not believe that his old protege and favourite was again false; and, ignorant of the plot formed | for his own overthrow between him, Maria Christina, and Louis Philippe, who was | already projecting the Spanish marriages, I freely allowed him to return. The price promised him for taking part in the insurrection of 1843 against Espartero's Government was the Governor-Generalship of Cuba. That promise was fulfilled ; and the world has learnt, from bluebooks and debates in Parliament, the manner in which this grasping satrap exercised his command, and the immense fortune he and his wrung from the blood of the mise- i rable race, the traffic in which his Government had been long bound by treaty to put an end to. On his return to Madrid O'Donnell, in right of his rank in the army, became a member of the Senate. Narvaez, whom he hated and who hated him, was then in

power. To his rule none, except a few Progresistas, dared to make the slightest opposition. O'Donnell announced that he was about to reinforce that Opposition, but he was silenced by the lucrative appointment of Director-General of Infantry. It was the place best suited for his future plans, as he could organise the army according to his pleasure. Narvaez soon saw the error he had committed, and he dismissed O'Donnell. Once more he rushed into the Opposition organised by Generals Concha, Serrano, &c., who accepted him as their leader. We remember the persecution O'Donnell suffered from the Sartorius Government; his concealment in Madrid ; his military insurrection; the combat of Vicalvaro; his defeat and retreat in Andalusia ; his utter failure and impotence; and the famous Liberal manifesto which dread of approaching destruction extorted from him, and in which he made an appeal to the people to rise in defence of their liberties. He offered them his sword, and flung himself into the ranks of the Liberal party. O'Donnell was defeated and flying when that appeal was made ; it was responded to by Espartero. Then, indeed, all was changed ; city after city, village after village, from south to north, from east to west, rose against the miserable crew who had oppressed, plundered, and degraded them. Espartero found the Queen besieged in her Palace in Madrid, and he saved her from public indignation by the prestige of his name, his honesty, and his popularity. Espartero carried his generosity and his

confiding spirit to a point which deserves censure. Never meaning bad faith himself, he did not suspect it iu others. He had saved O'Donnell from ruin; he now offered him the portfolio of War. How many times in the course of two years has not

Espartero covered his unpopular colleague with the buckler of his own honesty and his own influence! The presence of Espartero produced a restraint on the scandals of the Court; and it was by him and his, whom Maria Christina and her companions call the "enemies of the Throne," that that Throne has for the last two years been saved again and again. þÿ Paris Correspondent of the " Times."

From the London Times, August 2. A document of considerable importance as regards Parma, showing the desires of both Government and people there, has lately been partially published by a Turin paper. It is a memorial presented by Signov Molossi (a per son holding high employment under the Parma Government) on the part of a number of his fellow-citizens to the Regent, with her consent, and with the consent of her Ministers. Count Crenneville is said to have requested to be furnished with two copi s of it þÿ uno of which he sent to Vienna, and one to Marshal Radetzky. The memorial enters at great length into the state of the Duchy, past and present, its history, the law of succession of the Farnese Bourbons, the late crimes, and many other details of government. It ends by suggesting to the Duchess, as remedies for existing evils, 1st, to dismiss the present Director of Police, confiding this delicate branch of the service to a native of the country, cautious, temperate, prudent, devoted to the Prince, and to the laws of the State. 2d. To purge the police ofiices and disband that mob of officials, which has become hateful to the whole nation. 3d. To reorganize the army (most important). 4th. To recall the Parmesan prisoners from Mantua ( they are already said to be on their way back), to examine impartially into the cases of those condemned, and submit the others to a prompt and just trial. 5th. To raise the state of siege. 6tli. To cause the withdrawal of the Austrian troops. 7th. To repudiate resolutely the Custom-house league.

8th. To convoke under the Presidency of his Royal Highness the Extraordinary Council of State for secret deliberation on þÿ («) the equity of the. treaty of Florence of 1844 (which made a new adjustment of the territories of the Duchies on the demise of Maria Louisa) ; ( b ) the affair of the mines held by Baron Ward, &c. ; (c) the reduction of certain pensions enjoyed by favourites.

From the London Times, August 2. TURKEY. CONSTANTINOPLE, July 11. 1 wrote to you in my last of the difficulties which have arisen about the demarcation ot the frontier line of Bessarabia, and 1 have endeavoured to show that, if the labours ot the Bessarabian Frontier Commission are likely to meet with j great impediments and delays, the labours of the Asiatic Frontier Commission will be altogether fruitless. Since my last letter was written news has reached us which is likely to complicate the labours of both these commissions even more seriously. The Russians have occupied Serpents' Island, at the mouths of the Danube. 1 cannot tell what kind of an occupation it is, but the tact itself is quite certain, as well as that the 1 urkish Government has despatched a naval officer to ascertain the exact nature and all the circumstances of this Russian occupation. As this occupation will cause volumes of diplomatic correspondence, if nothing else, it will not be perhaps amiss to say something about the position in which Serpents' uninhabited the war. This island is an Island was before barren rock, to which the Russians laid claim in consequence of the Treaty of Adrianople. 1 hat island ; it says only in general terms, that " the treaty docs not make any special mention of this frontier line shall follow the course of the Danube as far as the embouchure ot St. George ; so that, leaving all the islands formed by the different branches of this river in the possession of Russia, the right bank will remain, as hereto-

fore, in that ot the Ottoman Porte and it adds that " it shall not be permitted to make any establishments or construct any fortifications upon the islands which shall remain in the possession of the Court of Russia, excepting always the quarantine buildings which shall be thereon established." Thus to claim Serpents Island according to the wording of this treaty was, to say the least, stretching its meaning to its bed ces, and pushing the river utmost consequen- rather far out into the sea. However, at that time Russia had it all her own way, and the territorial changes made by the treaty were so great, that the barr< n rock was altogether forgotten. For some years Russia did not make good her claim to it, and it remained deserted until in 1S33 she erected a lighthouse on the island, and sent there an invalid with his family, who had charge of it, and who served at the same time as a kind of symbol of Russian occupation. of the withdrawn in the beginning The invalid was war and the light extinguished. The Treaty of Paris, like the Treaty of Adrianople, forgot Serpents' Island, but, by giving it back to the Turks the mouths of the Danube, may be likewise supposed to have given them hack Serpents' Island, and they have latelyrestored the lighthouse. It was on the news of this, it is supposed, that the Russians have sent there some kind of force to occupy it. I hear the representatives of the Western Powers, as well as of Austria, have taken up the case very strongly, especially the representative

of the latter, which is not surprising, if we remember with what a jealous eye Austria has always watched the Russian preponderance on the Danube. Of course, this occupation may be explained in diplomatic language as a misun- ot derstanding" arising from overzealousness ,l some official ; but such facts, even it disavowed, cannot but create suspicious about the spirit in which Russia seems inclined to carry out the recent treaty, especially when such cases of au illiberal interpretation of the words of the treaty are not isolated. Nearly at the same time that the news of the Russian occupation of Serpents' Island reached us other news came from Asia evincing a similar spirit.

I told you bow the Russians may be said already to have eluded the intention of the allies to revise the Asiatic frontier by delaying to rej new their diplomatic relations with 1 urkey, upon which renewal the beginning of the labours ot the commission have been made dependent. They have not shown a more conciliatory spirit by blowing up the fortifications of Kara In consequence of this arbitrary interpretation of the treaty, orders were sent out from England to Colonel Yeates, the British Commissioner at Ei zcrouui, to send an officer to Kars, to ascertain what part of the fortifications had been blown up. The commissioner took some officers and went himself. But when they came to the Russian rayon they were s topped, aud told that they could not go further for, as long as a single English or French soldier remained on Turkish soil the Russians did not intend to give up their conquest, or allow any one to enter within their circuit. The allies thought it sufficient to restrict the Russian power in Europe, and leave it untouched in Asia. It was to he expected that the Russians would make the best of this. Indeed, it seems not at all unreasonable to suppose that their readiness to accept the terms of the allies was due in a great measure to the certainty that in so doing they would be left undisturbed on their most sensitive side. It cannot be too often repeated, that Russia's influence in Asia is essentially a moral influence, and this influence has not only not been impaired

by the war, but has rather increased. Persia was Russian influence so paramount in Never as lately. The Circassian deputation has departed Irom here with a heavy heart and a deep conviction of the power of Russia. The anxiety of Russia to keep the Kars territory up to the last moment has likewise no other object than the increase of this moral influence, especially on the Kurdish tribes. As she is the only channel of information for those people, she can easily make them believe that she came out victoriously of this as of her other wars against Turkey, and impressions of this kind produced on simpleminded people are not easily effaced, and will not be without their influence if, in spite of the assurances of the treaty, another war should arise.

Letters and < lommunications from Government : For Council's information, that a claim having been made for re-payment from this Landtreasury of ltd. 8 48 sk., expenses contingent on the sending out from Denmark pr. ship Triton, one 0. From the London Times. ITALY. Ti rin, July 28. The principal fact that has transpired since I last wrote concerning the attempted insurrection at Alassa is that which I telegraphed to you this morning þÿ viz., that the movement had been completely suppressed. How this happened, or in what manner the insurgents were dealt with by the Alodenese authorities, we are still without intelligence, for this is almost the only information vouchsafed from official sources, and there are none others as yet, since the telegraph, though repaired, is not available to private persons for the transmission of news on such subjects. With regard to the events of the night of the 23th, 26th, it appears that about 2 o'clock on the morning of the 26th some 60 persons from Sarzana and the neighbourhood collected near the frontier, opposite Parmignola, under the leadership of one llatti, of Santerenzio, the whole being unarmed. On pas.-mg the " Viva la Cailitu'.ime ! rispeU ite they Sardinian Gendarmes station 1 Carabinieri cried out, On the Modcncse territory they w re joined by a number of others, carrying arms themselves, and who, it is said, supplied arms to the new arrivals. They then directed their movements towards Carrara, disarming several Customhouse posts, pillaging the chest of the Parniignola station of 2,000 zwanzigers, and cutting the telegraph wires as they went. At Carrara they no doubt expected the ready to join them, but to find the p pulation true nature of their reception may he gathered from the fact that

the Sardinian Gendarmes arrested 21 persons in the course of Sunday who tried to cross the frontier into Piedmont with arms in their hands. The Genoese police have also been active the last few days, and have arrested some six or seven persons suspected of being concerned in this affair. That the Sardinian Government attaches very little importance to it is proved by Count Cavour not having thought it necessary to return to Turin even for a day in consequence, and when we see how completely isolated the attempt lias been, and how signally it has failed in disturbing the general tranquillity of the country, it must he admitted the Ministers have been justified in confiding in the good sense of tbe population instead of irritating people by searches and espionage. There can be no doubt now of the movement having enjoyed Alazzinian protection, though whether it was purely and simply a project of Alazzini is still unproved; but, whoever was the author, he deserves credit for his ingenuity in furnishing the ringleaders with constitutional watchwords, so as to induce people to believe the rising was favoured by the Sardinian Government, and fancy themselves betrayed when they found the Sardinian Government directly opposed to them, while at the same time it would afford Austria an opportunity of raising her usual complaint, that Piedmont her is the hotbed of revolution, and of extending occupation.

AMERICA. From the London Times N. Y. Correspondent. I would attempt to give a description of New York if in the limits of a letter it could be done with any success; but it would be as reasonable to attempt to describe London in the same space. Sinking all topographical details, dates, and history, therefore, a few of the more prominent characteristics of the place are all that can be at present noted. Those who fancy New York a mere busy provincial and commercial city þÿ a sort of Liverpool þÿ will be surprised to find it a great metropolis, unmistakably a capital, with many indications of immense wealth, and none of age, even of the age from which it dates. All is new, growing, and changing, as if the city itself partook of the ever extending tendencies of the country. Every renovation is 011 a larger and grander scale than what it succeeds, whether it be a mansion, an hotel, or a store. What the last fire spared is being rapidly demolished and replaced by something more equal to the requirements of the time. The amount of building now in progress is enormous, and for the moment rather inconvenient. In some streets, particularly near the business end of the city, every third house appears to have been pulled down ; and in a few months even a native is surprised at the change. Brick is becoming marble with wonderful celerity ; and the native marble, if well selected, is a beautiful building material ; it isas white as that of the Italian quarries which supply the statuary, and which we use for internal

decorations, but have not applied like common stone, except in the exceptional extravagance of the Marble Arch, and that is but a dingy affair. The smoke and fogs of London soon reduce everything to the line of mud ai d brick, or the dull compromise between them attempted by stucco. But in the clear air and brilliant sun of New York the purest material can be used with the certainty that it will preserve its colour. In the whole aspect of the city, as in the mode and manner of life, there is far more of what we should call "foreign" than of the specifically English. Except in language, religion, and laws þÿ three important exceptions, certainly þÿ our cousins have parteil company from us more widely than we are apt to suppose, or than is altogether pleasant t.i contemplate. The capital is much more like Paris, with a dash of Hamburg, than London; there is relatively a larger foreign population than in our metropolis, having much more political and social influence than with us, and the influence is distinctly marked. The style and habits of the most wealthy and populous city of the States are, no doubt, very different to those of the mass of the country; but it must have been a strong combination of causes that could have changed the descendants of the sober and somewhat stern English Puritans, who deemed gaiety, colour, music, and the theatre the prime snares of the Evil One, into a population with the characteristics of that of New York, delighting in outward decoration, orna-

ment, and gilding which we think so peculiarly southern. The street fronts blaze with gold inscriptions and signs, and the interiors of the shops are often fitted up in a style we should consider too gorgeous for business. The French cafe, which cannot exist in London, has taken root and flourishes with a splendour scarcely equalled on the Boulevards of Paris. The countless omnibuses that

s ru $ ft o ii ft ft v n s make the grand thoroughfare of Broad- I way almost impassable are light and gay in colour, panelled with paintings of flowers and fruit, and subjects " from the French" that would possibly shock j the eyes of Clapham ; in their place we | should have a scale of charges lor burial ! in a Necropolis, þÿ perhaps a wholesome, but not a cheerful reminder. The hotels are planned on a scale of size and fitted with a magnificence not yet attempted in London or Paris ; walking through their softly carpeted corridors, brilliantly lighted aid resplendent with mirrors and gilding, it is difficult to believe you are not in a palace prepared for a fete. You rather wonder the music does not strike up from the ballroom you seem to be approaching through such passages. This, however, is the style only of the newest creations; others, on a similar scale as to size, are more sober in adornment þÿ what we should call more businesslike. Some American moralists begin to be alarmed at the increase of luxury in this direction, and denounce this seductive splendour as likely to destroy all domestic habits and associations It is, perhaps, an open question. VVe have had the same arguments employed against the club system in London; the hotel life of America is very much the same thing, but including the ladies also; whether the extension is an improvement for the people themselves I will not venture to decide. I only know that to a stranger it appears a very agreeable feature. There are some things about the Ame-

rican metropolis which, though striking the eye less than its general lightness and love of ornament, from the shops of the region of traffic to the palatial mansions of the Fifth Avenue þÿ the Faubourg St. Germain of the capital þÿ are more deserving of praise and imitation. It is better supplied with water than any city in the world þÿ an inestimable blessing in this climate ; and the arrangement of the streets is so admirably simple it is impossible to lose your way after a little study of the plan, though the distances, it must be admitted, are perfectly Russian. The Broadway must be measured by miles. Luckily, omnibus rates are low, for, by an inexplicable adherence to a mode of conveyance we have abandoned, the old heavy hackney coach, double horsed and extortionate, still holds its place, and the light, handy cab of London is unknown. The private vehicles are mostly open and of the lightest possible build, running on mere rings with threadlike spokes þÿ the most fragile-looking things ever put together for locomotion. With their fast trotting horses, to which the youth of the city are much addicted, they fly along with perilous speed, quite in keeping with the national vividness of life þÿ with something, too, of the equally national disregard of it. I shall have to notice many other points in the external aspects of the city hereafter; the subject is not easily exhausted, neither is it old. What is always changing requires periodically to be described anew.

You will see by the papers that the citizens of San Francisco have deposed the State Government, or at least deprived it of all authority, and taken the execution of the laws into their own hands. It is the grandest development of the "Lynch" principle ever attained. But there appears to have been an imperative necessity for some process of the kind; the civil power had got into the hands of the " ticket-of-leave" class, and there was a license of crime that had become unendurable. It has been

put down by a combination of the respectable inhabitants, for any aid from the central power was out of the question. By the list of those hanged and deported by this irregular application of the strong arm of the law I regret to see that Ireland has contributed the largest portion of ruffianism it was a necessity to crush out of existence, or expel, in self-preservation. Of the two desperate murderers hanged by the Committee of Vigilance, one was a Casey ; the other most notorious ruffian, who would have met the same fate, but anticipated it by suicide, was a Sullivan ; in the 21) deported with a warning that it will be the worse for them if they ever return, 12 of the names are unmistakeahly Irish. In justice to the native Americans, the fact should be stated ; the "Know-Nothings" are not quite without justification in their avowed hostility to those who give them trouble There is nothing political in the movement in San Francisco. The committee will call a State convention, turn out the whole of the officers of the criminated Government, and elect a new one of better materials. As a specimen of what can be done with the ballot-box, the history of the deposed Government is very etlilying. Mr. Berkeley will not quote it in his next annual speech ; those who want a "frightful example" of the abuse of the system should read it up. The resolution for expelling Mr Brooks from Congrees for his assault on Mr. Sumner has been negatived by a majority of 20 ; .Mr Brooks announced

that the he had resigned his seat in order to appeal to his constituents; lie will most probably be re-elected. The trial of Mr. Herbert for the murder of the hotel waiter at Washington has not terminated.

CYCLONIC HURRICANES. A curious ami interesting Table of Cyclonic Hurricanes, which have occurred in the West Indies and the Atlantic Ocean, has boon reccntlv published by Mr. A. þÿl oey, of Havanna. The examination of these phenomena extends over a period of 362 years þÿ from 1493 to 1855 þÿ and the distibution of 355 hurricanes was as follows : þÿ January, 5 ; Feby., 7 ; March, 11 ; April, 6; May, 5 ; June, 10; July, 42; August, 96; September, 80; October, 69; November, 17 ; 1 tocemher, 7. Mr. Pocv observes, that although nothing is known of the causes which produce hurricanes or gales in any part of the world, vet it has now been proved by the examination and careful analysis of perhaps more than a thousand logs, and of some hundreds ot storms, that wind, in hurricanes and common gales on both sides the Equator, has two motions ; and that it turns or blows round a focus or centre in a more or less circular form, and at the same time has a straight or curved motion forward. þÿ Literary Journal.

AVe copy the following particulars from extracts in the St. Thomas þÿ þÿTidende : þÿ A dispatch, dated at New Orleans, August 1 4, says : þÿ A terrible storm occurred in this vicinity on Sunday which lasted all day, as also all day on Monday. Its effects, however, were most disastrous at Last Island, a great summer resort, and which our accounts represent to have been entirely inundated. Every building on the island is said to have been swept away, and no less than one hundred and thirty-seven lives are reported to have been lost ! The steamer Star, Capt. Smith, which left here on the 9th, Saturday, w ith a large number of passengers, encountered the storm before reaching Last Island, and became perfectly unmanageable þÿ she soon after became a complete wreck. The scene among the passengers was terrific, there being no less than 24 0 persons clinging to the wrecked fragments of the vessel, each anxiously waiting the arrival of some vessel to take them off. Caillon Island has also been submerged, but the accounts from thence are very meagre. It is reported, however, that an immense amount of property, and many lives have been lost. Altogether, the loss of property must be very heavy, but it is impossible, now, to calculate the, amount. The crops, it is feared, have also suffered severely.

Later. New Orleans, Aug. 1G. þÿ Nothing definite has yet been heard from Caillon Island, but there has undoubtedly been great loss of life there. It is reported that thirty bodies had been found on one end of the island. It is. supposed that at least ten thousand dollars in money, in pockets, fell into tier hands of the pirates on Last Island, and about five thousand dollars worth of baggage. The loss on this island is estimated at over one hundred thousand dollars. It is now believed that the number of lives lost by the dreadful storm of Sunday and Monday, will reach TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY , including men, women and children, but mostly the former. At Last Island alone, one hundred and ninety dead bodies have been found, the sight of which was terrible. The total loss of property by the sudden and unlooked-for calamity is computed at 8500,000, while sonic place it at a still higher figure.

THE CHOLERA!!! According to the latest accounts that we have received from St. Thomas, we learn that \ up to Wednesday, the 17th, there had been in all 206 cases of Cholera, with a mortality of ONE HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-EIGHT at that Island. To-day, we allude to the outbreak of this pestilential disease in the verdant i Isle of Madeira ; and in glancing over our files by the packet we find that in Sweden, as well as in America, the distemper had travelled. In Stockholm it had appeared with great severity, and General Bouisco, the Russian Military Envoy, was one of the first victims. At Staten Island (United States) it had broken out, and much alarm w-as felt at New York from the quantity of shipping in the harbor. Before concluding we may mention that we have heard Cholera has also appeared at our Sister Island, St. þÿJohn ; s we have no authentic information however. With these facts before us, and a reminiscence of our former preservation, we have much cause to be thankful for our continued protection ; and while we hope otherwise, let us make timely preparation to meet the monster should it visit our shores.

s T . H O IJ | A y l « Cholera at Madeira! We read in the þÿ Illustrated London News" of the 23rd August that this dreadful scourge þÿ now apparently traversing the universe þÿ had made its appearance at the Island of Madeira, hitherto one of the healthiest parts of the globe, and was doing the work of death and desolation. The account before us represents that the Epidemic prevails greatly, and seems likely to spread to all parts. Many persons had frightened themselves to death ! Drugs were scarce ; and one Chemist had to close his shop, owing to his stock of medicine being exhausted. In some places the crowd was so great that people had to wait for three or four hours for their turn to be served. The principal remedy used on first symptoms of the disease was camphorated spirits, essence of peppermint, laudanum and brandy. There was no scarcity of food in the Island, except meat, as the country people did not like bringing their cattle to town. On some days the number of deaths reached 11G. Out of a population of 15,000 inhabitants, over 2,000 had been carried off in less than a month. The British Government had dispatched a steamer from Portsmouth with medical aid, stores, and other comforts for the sick .

THE PACKET. On Sunday afternoon the mail-boat þÿ þÿFly arrived here with packet-letters and newspapers. The Mails were conveyed to Saint Thomas by the steam-ship þÿ þÿParana, which arrived there during Friday. We have not learnt the cause of the þÿSteamer sdetention. As we anticipated, the intelligence by the present mail is not important ; þÿaltho Europe is still in an unsettled state, ns our extracts will show, and the future portends some unhappy events. The affairs of Italy are said to be rapidly approaching a crisis ; Spain, we are j told, is on the high road to absolutism, and would, doubtless, have arrived there by this | time, but that the Queen is obliged to rememher that she reigns by virtue of a constitution ; | and another war with Russia is actually pre- I þÿ dieted. On this latter subject, the London I Weekly þÿDispatch says : þÿ þÿ We are sorry to | be obliged to hear what is the current talk of Government people and members of Parliament I still in town about Russia. They talk pretty loudly about another war. They allege that the prognostications of those who protested against the peace as only a truce in the interest ! of Russia have proved but too true, and that J the intelligence received from abroad makes it J but too plain that the Czar is practically I ignoring the whole important stipulations of the ! treaty. But it is looked upon as very doubtful whether France either will or can help us this time. She is deep in debt, and hints are not few that, as a depotic Sovereign, menaced by j

rival dynasties, he desires a good understanding with the Czar, the leader and champion of j absolutism. It is further alleged that as the war was not popular with the middle and higher classes of France, Napoleon will be fortified in support of a policy of neutrality by his subjects, especially by those who have hitherto been most disaffected by his dynasty." On the affairs of Italy, a letter from Naples asserts that þÿ France and England have addressed an ultimatum to the Government of the Two Sicilies, and that, in the event of a refusal to comply with their demands, their representatives are immediately to quit Naples. The demands are stated to comprise a general am- j nesty and administrative and judicial reform. \ The same letter adds that the King had consented to some concessions, but they have not appeared sufficient to the representatives of France and England, who have nevertheless referred the matter to their Courts. þÿ The amnesty granted by King Ferdinand is so unsatisfactory that even Austria has sent orders to Baron Hubner to continue on his mission, and make the most urgent representations. The sudden change is ascribed to the personal conduct of King Ferdinand himself, who, with the aid of stimulants, sits up night and day, and carries the Government on without the aid of his Ministers. The late rumour of his intended abdication is thought to have had a deep meaning. A clear connivance of Naples with the Montemolinist party in Spain has confirmed
the dissatisfaction of the Western Powers.

A most painful and exasperating narrative has been communicated to the Italian, French and English papers by M. Garibaldi. He relates the cruel þÿexecution murder, indeed, it should be þÿcalled of a fugitive party, headed by a Roman citizen, who went by the popular pseudonyme of Ciceroacchio, at Oontarina, near the mouth of the river Po. During the reforms and the revolutions in Rome Ciceroacchio was well known as a popular orator. His real name was Angelo Brunetti ; but the popular surname was given to him in virtue of his oratory, which was plain, powerful, and eminently calculated to lead a numerous public. He acted with the revolutionary party, and accompanied M. Garibaldi on the retreat from Rome in August 1849, but he did not carry arms. He was sup posed to have found safety by concealment in the Apennines. It is now said, however, that he was seized at Contarina by an Austian troop. He was accompanied by two sons, nineteen and thirteen years of age, and four other persons. From the London Weekly Dispatch. THE NEAPOLITAN ANSWER TO ENGLAND AND FRANCE. The Cologne Gazette publishes the following as a correct synopsis of the note of the King of Naples in reply to the recent notes of England and France : þÿ Ferdinand King formally declines all inter ference ot the Western Powers in the internal

affairs of his kingdom. He rejects it as con trary to all the rules of international law, as an attack upon the independence and dignitv of his Crown. Relying upon the principles of eternal justice, which prescribe þÿ that thou shalt not do unto thy neighbour what thou þÿwould st not have done unto þÿthee he puts the following questions to the London Cabinet, whose representations were made in much stronger language than those of France : þÿ þÿ What would Lord Palmerston say if the Neapolitan Government was to presume to des cribe the management of the English Cabinet, and to propose a modification in its internal policy, or the adoption ot more liberal views towards Ireland, or to recommend more humane conduct towards its Indian subjects ? What would he say þÿ what would he reply to the re presentatives of that Power which interfered in such guise with the Government of her Majesty ? He would reply, as the Court of Naples nowr replies, that he does not recognise in any one the right or the power to dictate a line ot conduct or to address reproaches. Or, rather, he would not do þÿthis Lord Palmerston would not even give himself the trouble to re ply at all ; he would most probably send the meddling representative his passpoits. And has not the King of Naples, as w'ell as Great Britain, the right to look after his own honour, and that of his people ? He may, as a proof of his goodwill, listen to communications made with a view to the consolidation of public order in Europe ; but then such communications must

be made with that moderation and deference which is due to a free and independent Sovereign ; and he alone must be allowed to form his judgment upon the propriety of the proposed measures, and of the moment for earning them out. No one except the King him self can form a correct judgment upon w-hat circumstances require. It is asserted that the present state of tilings requires certain alterations and improvements. It is stated that the armed attacks of the revolution against the Government of the two Sicilies have ceased This is prima facie evidence that the system opposed to them, and w-hich is the object of such violent attacks, is not so useless or so baneful as some persons w-ish it to be believed. But, it is added, the necessity for such a system no longer exists. The King is not of this opinion, and his will cannot be opposed unless the exercise of a superior force can be asserted as a right. But what will then become of the principle, of Royal authority ; and what value will be attached to the acts of Government w-hich have emanated under the pressure of a foreign Power? Under such circumstances any concession, however justifiable, would lose all effect. þÿ His Majesty King Ferdinand, therefore regards himself as perfectly justified in main-

taining his prerogative, and of notifying his intention to decide himself alone upon what ought to be done, and the proper time for doing it. He ardently desires that that time may speedily be at hand ; but it cannot be denied that the violent and systematical attacks of the English press and the demands thundered forth in the English Parliament are of a nature to ! adjourn that time for the present. It is supposed that such means are calculated to calm the evil passions in a country still a prey to the j revolutionary doctrines of 1848 1 It cannot | surely have been already forgotten that the Central Committee of Italy only recently established the principle < that political assassina- j tion was not a crime, especially when its object was to get rid of a powerful þÿenemy, and that this same committee puts a price upon the head of the King of Naples, and promised a reward of 100,000 ducats þÿ to the man who rid Italy of this þÿmonster. Considering such recent facts, it is not only the right, but it is the duty of his Majesty the King of the Two Sicilies, to act with the greatest caution, and not to relin- I quish carelessly a system of government which \ he thought fit to adopt, as much in the interest of his subjects as for his own safety. It has been asserted and attempts have been made to establish the assertion, that the Constitution of 1848, under which the above execrable pritici- j pies were openly promulgated, is the funda- j mental law of the kingdom of Naples. But it is overlooked that when that Constitution was j

proposed to the Sicilian Parliament they re- j jected it with contempt, and asked for the Constitution of 1812. The concessions then made by King Ferdinand II. had no other | effect than to increase the demands of the revolutionary faction throughout the whole of Italy, and the risings which took place at Naples and at Palermo were the signals for risings j in Sardinia, Rome and Lombardy. Is it desired to see a renewal of those dreadful crimes and catastrophes of which unhappy Italy was then the theatre ? The Constitution of 1848 would be wonderfully adapted to bring forward a repetition of them. þÿ But, on mature reflection, that cannot be rhc idea of the Cabinets of London and Paris, whose object must be the maintenance of the peace of Europe, so dearly bought. Especially \ it cannot be the view of the French Cabinet. After having taken such energetic measures at home to put down revolution, France surely cannot seek to create it in Italy. This would ; be in direct opposition to that wise aud clever j policy which has been so successfully carried j out. France and England should also remem- j ber that the war in the East was undertaken i precisely to prevent a foreign Power from in- ! terlering in the affairs of Turkey. Any simi- j lar interference in the kingdom of the Two Sicilies would be a curious anomaly, not to give i it a more precise qualification. King Ferdi- j nand cannot, and will not, believe in anything j of the sort. He places full confidence in the acknowledged principle so gloriously establish- |

cd by the Courts of Paris and London, accord- ! ing to which every independent State, although much weaker than the Power which wishes to I force its counsels upon it, has the ineontestible j right to reject those counsels if they contain a menace or an attack upon its independence. | The King is firmly resolved to adhere to what he has said. If, however, an attempt should j be made, which is scarcely possible, to go j further ( passer outre), his Majesty, relying on ! the justice of his cause, would appeal to the \ patriotism of his people, and, trusting to his i lirave and faithful army, would repel force bv i þÿforce. þÿ of the Seiue on From the Illustrated London News. RUSSIA The Kreuz Zeilung of Berlin is iuformed by a correspondent in London that, in the early part of last week, Lord Palmerston was in the receipt of a uote from the Russian Cabinet, in which þÿ the complaints of the English Government as to the manner in which Russia has carried out the stipulations of the treaty of peace, meet with a complete answer. From the London Times. Russia, though with a new Emperor and fresh opportunities, seems far from disposed to enter the path of reform. The obstinate and sullen spirit still lives humiliations are, it would appear, þÿ almost already forgotten, and both Czar

S T . ® & ® E I AVI® . and people are as ready as ever to play j the old game of pride, violence, and j cunning, which was successful for more I than 150 years. But we cannot think that at the present time such a display will be successful. Common prudence ; would advise a more gradual and less | demonstrative return to the assumptions and menaces of former days. It is but a few months since Russia accepted the terms of peace proposed through Austrian mediation. At that time we were told daily by the Russian press in Europe of the sincerity and moderation of j the Czar, To believe certain prints j and certain politicians, Russia was a j land of good faith, and her unambitious j people were losi in astonishment, at the designs imputed to them by the mis- | guided Cabinets of the West. About last February, when the representatives of Europe were to meet in Paris, the tone of every Russian organ was most magniloquent and high-minded. Peace, goodwill to all men, popular instruction, railways, canals, improved agriculture, free trade, were in the heart ofevery Russian. A smile of good-humoured pity was the answer to those who hinted that Muscovite policy might still remain unchanged, and that it would be as well to take guarantees while we were still strong, united, and in earnest. All this lasted until peace was made, and Russia obtained conditions with which she had no reason to be dissatisfied. Now, however, all is changed. Cronstadt is no longer threatened; Poland is for ever abandoned by the West, and will be

fully Russianized before war again visits Europe; Bessarabia, with the exception of a narrow slip, is preserved; the Caucasus still remains a Russian possession. The Czar is about to be crowned with much splendour, and all Europe is flocking to the sight. Russia is again taking her stand as a great Power, and is no longer a vast prison, with a Sovereign, nobility, and people placed under the ban of the world. Hence the old, inveterate obstinacy, revives ; the old cunning is once more to he tried to discover if it can, as of yore, command success. There can he no doubt of the unwillingness of Russia to cede quietly ai d honourably what has become by treaty the property of the Ottoman Slate. We shall, perhaps, have it explained with many details that the difficulties we complain of were unavoidable; that the destruction of Kars and the Dariuhian forts was strictly legal, and that the occupation of Serpents Island was only some transaction connected with the lighthouse. But facts still remain on record. It is certain that the conduct of the Russians has induced England again to occupy the Black Sea. The Hannibal has been sent to Serpents Island, and sufficient intimation has been given that in the opinion of the allies something like a breach of faith has taken place. Compare the conduct of France and England with that of their late enemy. The allies had more than 250,000 men in the East. They had prepared, far from their own country, immense stores of food, clothing, and

warlike material, in expectation of long . hostilities. Every man and horse and j gun had to be brought away by sea, at a time when transport was scarce and dear. Yet in four months, two-thirds of the time allowed, not only the Crimea j but Turkey itself has been cleared of I the allied troops. We learn from Con- ; stantinople to-day that after the depar- | ture of a flotilla then about to sail scarcely a thousand Frenchmen would

be left in Turkey. Our own naval and military establishments have been broken up, and soon Scutari will retain no traces of us except the graves of the dead and the monument which commemorates them. This promptness, so honourable to both nations, has not been imitated by Russia. Although Kars is but some 30 miles from her own frontier, and held but by a few thousand men, she is there still, destroying works, cutting down forests, refusing English officers the right of visiting the spot, and, during her little term of power, playing the despot after the fashion of Warsaw or Tiflis. 'file same is the case at the mouth of the Danube. Russian troops are still there, and will remain until the latest day allowed by treaty, with perhaps the desperate hope that something will happen to enable them to refuse the cession altogether. The part of Bessarabia which is to be added to the Principalities is still in Russian hands, and the Czar raises doubts on the topography, and would, as far as may be judged from appearances, gladly evade the condition which for the first time causes his frontier to recede. We do not certainly think that any practical result will follow from these litigious ami undignified displays. The other Powers are far too much in earnest to allow any trifling in matters of such importance. 1< will be observed that Austria, who perhaps knows her neighbour better than we do, has not yet evacuated the Principalities, although she ought to have done so some time since. She is, no doubt, waiting until

Russia shall have performed her part of tin engagement. That when the end of the six months comes we shall see the R issi ms unwillingly depart is certain enough. We may in future times have to watch their designs for the recovery of their former territory, hot that they will acquiesce for the present We know, because we have tile power to enforce it. But the spirit of the Court of St Petersburg is not the less apparent. |t can hardly he to impose on civilized nations that the Russian Sovereign makes this display of ini potent obstinacy. Indeed, the impression it must leave on Europeans is rather that Russia is weaker and more sorely wounded than was thought. To see her lingering at the spots she must leave, and performing acts of paltry tyranny to the last, cannot raise her in the eyes of German or Italian. But it may be that on some ignorant and con filling races the spectacle of her armed occupation after the allies have left the East may have an influence. If she hold Kars after France and England have withdrawn their armies from Constantinople, the fact may he explained consistently with Russian interests among nations to whom Russia alone speaks. Nevertheless, in the end such subterfuges can he of little avail, and the conduct of Russia, by destroying any nascent feeling of confidence among the Western nations, will bring on her evils far overj balancing any advantages which a dila tory evacuation can procure.

Iron Lighthouse for the Bahamas The British Admiralty have very lately caused to be constructed by Messrs. Grissell, j of Hoxt.on, a Cast Iron Lighthouse, intended j to be erected on the Great þÿIsaac Rock, s on the j Bahama Bank. The Lighthouse, which was ! commenced in June 1855, and completed in j the beginning of this year, is 124 feet in height, i exclusive of a large revolving lantern, 15 feet j high, which surmounts the tower ; its diameter j is 25 feet at the base, and 14 feet at the top ; the total weight of metal used in its construction is about 300 tons, and the cost of the whole is estimated at <£8,000. The building is divided into seven compartments or floors, each | 16 feet in height. The first is fitted up as a j kitchen ; the second will be used as a sitting room ; the third as a bedroom, and the remain- j ing stories upwards are to be devoted to purposes connected with the main object of the structure þÿ as a beacon to mariners navigating a perilous gulf in the Atlantic. The interior of the apartments is lined with corrugated iron to diminish the heat of a tropical climate, and the building is pierced all round at short intervals with small glazed loop-holes for the purposes of i light and ventilation The lantern contains 21 burners, all showing white lights, except one, which is red, and each of them strongly intensified by brilliant reflectors of copper, thickly coated with silver. Seven or eight men will be employed to keep the light burning in this tower. While on the subject of Lighthouses, we may

take the opportunity of again expressing our surprise that the attention of the Admiralty, or even commercial nations, has not yet been directed to the erection of a similar building on the Anegada, one of the British Virgin Islands, situated to the eastward of Tortola. The vessels of all nations traverse those waters, and every mariner will join with us in pronouncing the Anegada reefs among the most perilous in the Caribbean seas. The land is so very low, and the reefs run out to such a distance, that vessels are actually upon the latter without knowing þÿ there to be met by a horde of pirates, who, instead of rendering succour, endeavour to demolish the unfortunate vessels and rob their cargoes.

THE CHOLERA!!! (From the St. Thomas Times, September 20.) The official announcement contained in our columns to-day in connexion with Sporadic Cholera, is much more encouraging than we have in one or two previous instances been enabled to place before the public. It will there be seen that six new cases have transpired during three days, whilst only two deaths have occurred. The total of mortality numbers 180, and there being no cases or deaths to-day, we trust that that long wished-for period when we may, with certainty, pronounce the disease as having disappeared, is at length about to arrive. Up to Monday, the 22nd instant, there had been 183 deaths from Cholera at St. Thomas, out of 221 cases. þÿ Editor Avis.

This document is a remarkable one, upon more grounds than one. It is remarkable for its length, and for the elaborate and careful manner in which every possible aspect of the question involved is discussed ; contrasting favourably, in this respect, with the vague generalities with which the Plenipotentiaries at Paris so hastily disposed of the question in the midst of the bustle of their final sittings. It is still more remarkable, however, for the arguments employed, and for the reasons alleged by the United States for acquiescing in some and dissenting from others of the propositions contained in that Declaration. One guiding principle in their diplomacy avows itself throughout the whole context of this paperþÿ namely, that abstract and general motives of humanity are not sufficient grounds to induce a State to abandon any part of its belligerent rights ; and that, in prudence, it ought not to do so without þÿ compensating þÿadvantages. it concedes. The Great Comet of 1856. þÿ If the accounts from Limerick are to be credited, the marvellous comet of 1556, after an absence of just three centuries, has made its predicted reappearance in the South of Ireland. The Limerick Observer, of Saturday, says : þÿ þÿ A gentleman of the highest respectability has just informed us that he saw lust night, for the third rime, what appears from his description to be the longexpected comet of 1856, the re-appearance of whicli this year has been so long foretold ; astronomers, however, guarding their calcula ions by the proviso that a difference of three years might possibly occur, although there was every reason to expect that the great comet, which takes three centuries to complete its orbit, would be visible about the month of August, 1856. Our informant thus describes the object which attracted his attention for the lirst lie was standing near the salmon-weir, on the platform before the mills of Corbally, about, half-past 10 þÿo clock, when his attention was attracted by what appeared to be a fire

East of his position. lie remarked the object to a gentleman who was with him, but, as the (ire rose and cleared the top of the mountain, his friend suggested that it must be a lantern suspended to a kite. It had then the appearance of a globe of fire as large as a good-sized orange, with a broad tail of light extending about 18 inches from the body. The two gentlemen watched it lor about an hour, and the watchman on the weir observed it also. On Thursday night they all saw it again. It rose a few minutes later, presenting the same appearances, and was high in the heavens at half-past 1 1 þÿo clock, when they went home. At that hour one of the gentlemen pointed it out to his sister. Last night, from the same place, the same per sons again saw it rise about 20 minutes before 11 þÿo clock, and then it first occurred to one of them (our informant) that it might he a comet. lie ceased to watch it about midnight, hut the watchman observed it up to half-past 1 this morning. It. did not seem so large as on the previous nights, but still far exceeded the most brilliant form in which the planet Jupiter has ever been beheld. As the greatest comet on record is really due about this time, and as the extreme sultriness of the weather would seem to warrant the belief that such a celestial visitor is near at hand, we shall be glad to hear if any other persons have observed the appearance which has thrice risen upon our astonished þÿfriends.
